summary: Solana trade costs split into the 5,000-lamport-per-signature base fee, the compute-unit-price priority fee, optional Jito bundle tips, swap and pool fees with slippage and price impact, MEV (sandwich) losses, perp funding and borrow costs, and refundable account rent; this pack catalogues 208 cited sources across 8 facets plus contested. Evidence status: research claims ungated (v4 evidence gate not passed); treat as leads with cited sources.

facts.text: SIMD-0553 is not active. Its status is Draft in the SIMD repository (created 2026-06-03, one commit, merged 2026-07-20), none of its three feature accounts (resource_fee_burn_1_10, resource_fee_burn_1_4, resource_fee_burn_1_2) exists on mainnet on 2026-11-06, and live fee probes still return 5,000 lamports per signature. The solana-sdk FeeDetails type already has a resource_fee field marked 'Introduced with SIMD-0553', so client code is prepared.

QuickNode's qn_estimatePriorityFees is an add-on method. last_n_blocks defaults to and is capped at 100, an optional account scopes it to a program, and api_version 2 is described as 'more accurately weighted'. It returns per_compute_unit and per_transaction levels low (25th percentile), medium (50th), high (75th) and extreme (90th), a percentiles map in 5-point steps, and a 'recommended' value described as 'to maximize chances of landing'. QuickNode couples fee and routing: non-duplicate transactions sent with the recommended fee or higher are routed through its staked (SWQoS) connection. Its

A sendBundle success response means the Block Engine received the bundle, not that it landed. The result is a bundle ID (the SHA-256 of the transaction signatures). Users report a returned ID with nothing on Solscan. Check getInflightBundleStatuses (Pending, Landed, Failed or Invalid, last 5 minutes) and getBundleStatuses (null if not found or not landed).

Triton One, Bitwise and SOL Strategies are the first third-party BAM node operators. They start on testnet (announced 2026-11-02). Access for any mainnet validator is targeted for early Q1 2027. Helius's 2025 explainer said BAM aims for 50 to 100+ nodes.

The tip is any instruction that transfers SOL to one of 8 Jito tip accounts, fetched with getTipAccounts. Jito advises picking one at random to reduce contention and keeping tip accounts out of Address Lookup Tables. Tips do not prioritize a transaction at validators that are not Jito-Solana leaders.

Slippage is the gap between the quoted output and what the wallet actually receives, and it grows with time between quote and execution. Jupiter says it depends on pair volatility, trade size relative to pool liquidity and the time between quoting and execution; Raydium says it is a function of latency, concurrent transactions and block inclusion order.

Swap V2 /order is a meta-aggregator. Metis (Jupiter's onchain multi-hop, multi-split router), JupiterZ (off-chain RFQ market makers), Dflow and OKX all quote, and the best execution price wins. /build uses Metis only. Jupiter says RFQ quotes often beat onchain routing by 5 to 20 bps on major pairs but publishes no data for that range.

On Pacifica and Velocity, positive funding (perp above oracle/index) means longs pay shorts, and negative funding means shorts pay longs. This contrasts with Jupiter JLP markets, where longs and shorts both pay the pool and nobody receives funding.
Pacifica, Hyperliquid, Velocity and Jupiter's Beta markets all settle funding hourly. A positive rate means longs pay shorts; a negative rate means shorts pay longs.

Solana rent is a one-time, fully refundable minimum-balance deposit, not a recurring fee. An account must hold (128 + data_len) x lamports_per_byte lamports. The 128 is fixed storage overhead. Closing the account returns the whole deposit to the destination the closer names. Rent exemption is no longer time-based: SIMD-0194 (Activated) renamed lamports_per_byte_year to lamports_per_byte and fixed exemption_threshold at 1.0.

The automatic state-growth controller (SIMD-0389) is not in force. Its pull request was closed unmerged by the stale bot on 2026-07-21, and SIMD-0438 calls the controller 'yet to be accepted'. SIMD-0437 still says SIMD-0389 'does this automatically'. The only reset path today is the manual SIMD-0438 gate. In review, two reviewers agreed to keep the controller out of the prerequisites for step 3. This status is inferred from the closed pull request.

SIMD-0438 is the manual rollback: a feature gate that resets lamports_per_byte to the legacy 6,960 and 'should only be activated in response to excessive state growth observed on mainnet beta'. Firedancer's feature map lists it as set_lamports_per_byte_to_6960 (key rnt8ZQpz2HYhX3DkYBDGjJS1a36mYq69oXka7JrhEdi). That gate account did not exist on mainnet on 2026-11-06. After a reset, an account that was reclaimed stays valid only if it does not grow, change owner or fall below its starting balance.

The party that funds a token account is not the party that gets the refund. A sender can create the recipient's associated token account inside a transfer and pays its rent; the owner or close authority later picks the close destination. Jumpbit reports a self-measured case: 37 spam-token accounts funded by scammers (0.075 SOL) were burned and closed by the wallet owner, who kept the rent.

Attack structure moved from tight (adjacent) sandwiches to wide ones that span transactions, slots or blocks. The arXiv study reports tight sandwiches at 54-87% of attacks before the Marinade blocklist, 18% in the Marinade era and 1% after the JitoSOL delisting; 96% of attacks in the final era span blocks. A Ghostlogs talk summary reports wide (blind) sandwiching rising from about 1% to 30% of attacks in recent months. Detectors limited to a single slot or to Jito bundles miss wide attacks.

jitodontfront works as follows. The transaction includes any valid public key starting with 'jitodontfront' in an instruction. The account need not exist on chain. The Jito block engine then rejects any bundle that contains the transaction unless it sits at index 0. Jito's own docs say it 'may help reduce sandwich attacks but is not guaranteed to do so' and 'applies only to the block engine and not to any other software'.

Where a tip goes, step 1: tips sit in the eight tip PDAs until the leader's validator calls the Tip Payment Program. The program's own comment says the validator should call change_tip_receiver before executing any transaction that contains tips, and again if it detects a fork. The call drains all eight accounts, pays block_builder_commission_pct percent of the total to the block builder (the value is at most 100, is set by change_block_builder, and is 0 after initialize), and sends the remainder to the tip receiver. In Jito's design the receiver is the validator's per-epoch TipDistributionAcc

Routing-layer validator exclusion is now a mainstream defense. Helius MEV Protect is opt-in per request (mev-protect=true, off by default), avoids leaders statistically linked to sandwiches in their own or adjacent blocks, excludes roughly 3-4M SOL of stake at a time, works with sendTransaction, sendBundle and Sender, and leaves tip and priority-fee requirements unchanged. Axiom's recommended 'Secure' setting also limits submission to a validator whitelist (Heimbach et al.), and Helius says apps can set their own allow or deny lists.

SIMD-0553 is still status Draft in the SIMD repo: it was merged on 2026-07-20 and has had no commit since (repo head 2026-11-02). Agave's implementation PR 14275 was closed unmerged on 2026-10-08 by a maintainer, hours after the stale bot labeled it, and no successor PR turned up; neither Agave master nor Firedancer contains resource-fee logic. Its governance wrapper SGP-0003 crossed the 65.16M SOL signaling threshold on 2026-08-05, which started an 11-epoch vote that Solana Compass said would close on 2026-08-18; no result was found. Protocol and market-structure defenses were still early in Jan 2025 (Helius). Sandwich-resistant AMMs (Ellipsis Labs' audited Plasma reference design) neutralize intra-slot sandwiches but leak at slot boundaries when one leader holds consecutive slots. RFQ routes such as JupiterZ (default from Dec 2024) avoid slippage and MEV but suit widely traded tokens. Paladin ran on 80 validators (6% of stake). Multiple concurrent leaders were judged years away.

Pool-level trading fees are a second cost layer inside every routed hop and differ by venue. Raydium CPMM and CLMM expose 21 on-chain fee configs each (0.005% or 0.01% up to 4%, default 0.25%, admin-extensible), and Raydium's own CLMM page lists only four typical tiers and says to confirm live via the clmm-config API. Orca Whirlpools tiers run 0.01% to 2%.

Jupiter's documented platform fee on Swap V2 /order (and on the earlier Ultra API) depends on the pair: 0 bps when buying JUP, JLP or jupSOL with SOL or a stablecoin; 0 bps for pegged pairs (LST-LST, stable-stable); 2 bps for SOL-stable; 5 bps for LST-stable; 10 bps for everything else; 50 bps for tokens under 24 hours old. Jupiter takes the fee in one mint chosen by priority (SOL, stablecoins, liquid staked tokens, bluechips, others) and reports it as feeMint, with the total rate in feeBps and its own part in platformFee.feeBps. Six keyless quote-only /order calls on 2026-11-06 at small test

A swap's cost splits into separable layers: (1) the aggregator or integrator fee, (2) the trading fee of every pool in the route, since each hop pays its own, (3) price impact against pool depth, and (4) quote-to-fill slippage; network fees (base, priority, tips) are a further layer. Jupiter's /execute response isolates layer 1: if feeMint is the input mint the fee is totalInputAmount - inputAmountResult, and if it is the output mint the fee is outputAmountResult - totalOutputAmount (documented example: 2103 - 2101 = 2 output units).

A Mar 28, 2026 Crypto News Navigator article claims Raydium beat Jupiter by 0.05% to 0.25% on $1,000 to $15,000 swaps, with Jupiter within a few bps below $500 and sometimes ahead above $20,000. The evidence is 100 swaps 'executed by community members on Solana forums', with no data, method or venue-level breakdown, and the article is inconsistent about which pairs were sampled and mixes revenue periods. It is not usable as a benchmark; it also does not test whether Jupiter's 2 to 10 bps platform fee explains part of any gap.

A Solana perp position pays up to four application-layer costs on top of the SOL network fee: a per-fill trading fee, a holding cost (funding, or a pool borrow fee), interest on any borrowed collateral, and a liquidation charge. Jupiter's and Velocity's docs list all four as separate items. Pacifica documents fees, funding and borrow interest on separate pages.

The JLP-market price impact fee has two parts. The linear part rounds up to whole basis points, so every trade pays at least 0.01%; at October 2026 parameters SOL adds 0.01% per started ~$375,000 of size. The additive part applies only when a trade enlarges the roughly one-minute net long-minus-short flow beyond a per-asset threshold ($1.5M on SOL and ETH, $750,000 on wBTC). Base, linear and additive fees together cap at 0.50% of trade size, so the price impact fee is at most 0.44%.

Blacklists removed one exposure signal but did not stop the attacks. In the arXiv study the share of attacks in over-represented leaders' slots fell from 50% to 2% across the interventions, while daily volume settled near 20,000 and attacks moved to wide, cross-block forms and to the application layer. Marinade said sandwichers 'spun up new validators faster than we could identify and block them', and a Marinade forum post of 14 May 2025 says attackers change identity addresses and open new validator instances. Anza's Max Resnick credits better Solana code, not blacklisting, for the fall in sa

A perp trading exactly at its oracle price still carries a baseline funding of about 0.00125% per hour, which is 10.95% a year on notional. Pacifica and Hyperliquid fix the interest component at 0.01% per 8 hours, and Velocity adds an offset of oracle TWAP / 3333. Hyperliquid's docs say this baseline is paid to shorts and quote it as 11.6% APR. Gauntlet's 2025-01-30 table shows Hyperliquid at +10.95% for SOL, BTC and ETH.

On Pacifica, Phoenix and Velocity, funding is not zero when the perp trades at the oracle price. Each builds in a fixed interest term of 0.01% per 8 hours (0.00125% per hour; 10.95% APR simple, 11.6% compounded) that longs pay to shorts. Phoenix writes F = m x [P + clamp(I - P, -R, R)] with I = 0.01% per 8 hours (m = 1 and R = 0.05% for crypto). Pacifica uses the same structure with a 0.05% clamp and divides by 8. Velocity adds a floor of oracle TWAP / 3333 (10.95% annualized) before its hourly conversion. Hyperliquid documents the same 0.01% per 8 hours term and the same formula structure.

Published fee schedules are not what every trader pays on every date, because venues run temporary promotions. Drift's July 2025 fee-structure post announced a limited-time 0% taker and maker campaign on BTC-PERP and ETH-PERP. SolanaFloor reported that Pacifica temporarily halved all trading fees in September 2025, and a KuCoin item dated 2025-11-11 tied a five-fold volume rise to $1B a day to that halving. Pacifica also cut SPCX fees 69% from 2026-06-12 to 2026-06-18. Pacifica's fee page mentions none of these.

Part of the relaunched Drift/Velocity exchange's net revenue flows to a recovery pool each quarter until inflows equal the $295,426,725.97 April 2026 exploit loss. Tether committed up to $127.5M and partners up to $20M.

A pipeline that finds priority fees by scanning for ComputeBudget instructions records zero for v1 transactions, because a v1 message has no ComputeBudget instruction and its account keys omit the ComputeBudget program. Readers must branch on the version byte and read transactionConfig instead. QuickNode's audit script shows meta.fee as the total: a v1 transaction with a 5,000-lamport priority fee and one signature reports totalFee 10,000.

Estimator output is sensitive to whether zero-price samples are counted, because most transactions set no meaningful priority fee. Bitquery reports that the median sits at the base fee, the quartiles sit at or barely above it, and the distribution lifts only in the last percentile or two. Helius counts non-vote transactions with no compute-unit price as zero samples, which is why Min and Low often return 0, and says percentiles over priced transactions only would be higher at every level. solfees exposes a skipZeros flag for the same choice. The same market can therefore yield very different n

A higher CU price does not guarantee landing. During the April 2024 memecoin congestion, Phantom's developer-relations manager said priority fees 'are not working as expected and adding a higher fee does not result in improved success rates.' Landing probability belongs to the priority-fee estimation concept, not this one.

Gasless swaps cost extra: when the taker holds under 0.01 SOL, Jupiter raises the swap fee by the USD value of the SOL it fronts (network fee, priority fee or tip, ATA and other rent). The added cost is a fixed amount, not a percentage, so small trades suffer most; the minimum trade is about $10 and the increase shows up in feeBps. Passing integrator parameters (referralAccount, referralFee, payer) or manual-mode parameters disables gasless.

Gasless swaps cost extra through the swap fee. When the taker holds under 0.01 SOL and the trade is about $10 or more (the minimum is dynamic), Jupiter's sponsor wallet pays gas and rent, and the swap fee rises by the USD value of that SOL, converted into the traded token. The surcharge is a fixed amount, so small trades pay proportionally more. The docs' example is a 5 bps platform fee plus 7 bps of gasless recoup, shown as feeBps 12. Automatic sponsorship does not fire when referral parameters are set. When JupiterZ wins the route, the market maker pays network and priority fees at no extra

Worked overpay example: a swap that consumed 75,000 CUs but declared 1,400,000 CUs at 50,000 micro-lamports/CU paid a 70,000-lamport priority fee. Oversized limits can also make the scheduler defer a transaction when a hot account nears its per-block write-lock CU cap. The author sells a swap-routing product.

Validators and stakers receive tips through Jito's tip distribution program. Each epoch the validator client opens a TipDistributionAccount derived from the epoch and the vote account. After the epoch, an off-chain process builds a merkle tree of claims and uploads its root on-chain: the validator gets its MEV commission share and stake accounts split the rest pro rata. Claimants redeem with merkle proofs. Under the TipRouter NCN, node operators compute the roots and upload one once 2/3 of stake agrees. Since JIP-16 the TipRouter also distributes priority fees.

Uncled blocks can unbundle a bundle. When a leader's block is skipped, any party that received it can rebroadcast its transactions. Those transactions enter the normal banking stage, which ignores bundle atomicity and revert protection, so they can land or revert on chain individually. Jito's mitigations: add pre- and post-account checks, and keep the tip in the same transaction as the strategy so a failed transaction does not pay the tip.

Keep a second path. Jito's DBI notes say to keep the Block Engine as a fallback because DBI serves BAM leader slots only and pauses during BAM node maintenance. Jito planned to put every mainnet BAM node into Maintenance Mode before the Alpenglow upgrade, with DBI users told to use the legacy Block Engine path. RPC Fast describes production senders fanning out to several Block Engine regions plus other relays, with raw RPC as a degraded fallback.

Common estimation mistakes named by vendors: using a global network-wide estimate (Helius: paying a global VeryHigh 'usually means overpaying by a wide margin'; OrbitFlare: wrong for contested accounts and costly on quiet ones); cranking a blanket fee during 'network congestion' when the contention is local (RPC Fast); keeping library-default compute limits, which inflate the fee and, per OrbitFlare, rank the transaction lower with the scheduler; fixed fees that go stale within hours; and bidding to fix delivery for a transaction that never reaches the leader.

On the Block Engine path a bundle must carry a tip of at least 1,000 lamports (0.000001 SOL), or the API rejects it with 'Bundle must tip at least 1000 lamports' (seen in gist comments in March and June 2025 when the tip was undefined). Jito warns that the floor can be too low to win the auction when demand is high, so contested opportunities need higher tips. The tip is a SOL transfer, in any instruction (top-level or CPI) of any transaction in the bundle, to one of the 8 tip accounts. Jito advises picking the account at random to reduce contention.

Jupiter Ultra's low exposure is not a clean measure of protection. Heimbach et al. measure a median excess ratio of 0.7 (2.0 counting single-victim sandwiches only) but say Ultra routes less long-tail token flow, which also lowers exposure. Jupiter credits Ultra V3 (17 Oct 2025) private routing and dynamic slippage and claims '34 times' better sandwich protection; that is a vendor claim, not a result of the study. Ghost also attributes low impact on Jupiter and Phantom to different order flow, routing and user profiles.

Splitting a large order within one minute on Jupiter's JLP markets does not avoid the additive price impact fee. The fee measures all net flow on the asset over roughly the last minute, including the trader's own trades and liquidations.

Solana prices contention per piece of state (local fee markets). Transactions compete when they write the same account, so a hotspot raises fees only for transactions touching it. A blanket high fee during network-wide congestion is therefore often wasted on uncontested accounts.

Bundles and tips help only when the slot leader runs Jito-compatible software. The Block Engine forwards winners only to a leader running Jito-Solana, and Jito warns that tips do not prioritize transactions at non-Jito leaders, so such a tip is a waste of money. A sender can check the schedule first: the gist's example loops on getNextScheduledLeader and sends only when a Jito leader is within 2 slots.

The base fee is signature_count x lamports_per_signature, with lamports_per_signature fixed at 5,000. signature_count includes the transaction's Ed25519 signatures plus signatures checked by the Ed25519, Secp256k1 and (when enabled) Secp256r1 precompiles.

A transaction pays its fee even when it fails. The fee is deducted from the fee payer before execution, and a transaction that fails while loading accounts can still be committed as fee-only (ProcessedTransaction::FeesOnly in Agave): the payer is debited the full total fee although nothing executes. Firedancer carries the same case as the flag FD_TXN_P_FLAGS_FEES_ONLY.

Transaction v1 went live on mainnet when feature txv1aq4pp281K9um3tnPgkfX8UqtFT6wcVW3hNezGLL activated at slot 447,120,000, the first slot of epoch 1035, at block time 2026-09-15T01:04:23Z. Testnet activated at epoch 1025 on 2026-09-01. RPC nodes need Agave 4.2.2 or later. v1 raises the size cap from 1,232 to 4,096 bytes (SIMD-0296), drops address lookup tables and allows up to 64 inline accounts. Legacy and v0 transactions still work.

When account keys are passed, Agave returns for each slot the larger of the block minimum and the highest minimum fee recorded for any of those writable accounts (a std::cmp::max over per-account minimums). An account's minimum is kept only if it exceeds the block minimum, and only writable accounts are tracked. Agave's own struct comment calls this 'the minimum fee needed to land a transaction'. Chainstack draws the practical consequence: each returned value is a floor, so an average or median of the values is an average or median floor, not the fee actually paid.

Solana prices contention per writable account, not network-wide. Transactions compete when they write the same account, so a hot account raises fees only for transactions that touch it. Agave's cache records minimum fees per writable account. Helius docs say 'Solana prices priority fees per writable account'. RPC Fast and OrbitFlare tell builders to estimate from the accounts their transaction writes, not from network-wide medians. A blanket high fee during network-wide congestion is therefore often wasted on uncontested accounts.

Handle retries on the client. Rebroadcast the same signed bytes every couple of seconds until the transaction confirms or its blockhash expires, and track lastValidBlockHeight (Triton: the transaction can land up to lastValidBlockHeight + 1). Do not re-sign with a new blockhash until getBlockHeight is above that value and getSignatureStatuses shows the original absent, because both signed versions can execute. Treat a transaction as landed at confirmed or finalized, since a processed transaction can be dropped on a minority fork. Triton says maxRetries has no effect on its endpoints. QuickNode

For the stock RPC, Chainstack recommends taking the maximum of the non-zero returned values (or a high percentile such as p95) over the 150-slot window and multiplying by an urgency factor of about 1.5 for normal load and 3 or more when racing for the same accounts. No source publishes a measured landing rate for this recipe.

Whether a higher fee improves landing depends on the congestion regime and the submission path. In March 2024 Phantom's developer-relations lead Brian Friel said priority fees were 'not working as expected' and that 'adding a higher fee does not result in improved success rates' (crypto.news, 2024-03-22). In April 2024 Helius CEO Mert Mumtaz said raising fees was not a workable fix, because much of the spam happens before scheduling (Cryptometer, 2024-04-05). Chorus One's observational data from its own validator's slots (2024-11-18 to 2024-11-25) found that priority-fee size 'generally doesn'

A landed-only sample understates the competition, because the bids that lost never enter it. Raiden's guide treats the failed attempts' bids as the competitor set and suggests bidding above the failed side's upper percentile (it uses the failed p90 on whichever dimension decides inclusion), using short windows (it recommends 5 minutes before sending). Its congestion index is the failed share of buys on a 0-100 scale, and one sample (as of 2026-07-22) showed 82.9. This works only for failures that reached the chain. Sweep timing is cheap either way. The fee is per transaction, not per account: 116 accounts need 6 transactions at the 5,000-lamport base fee, or about 250 lamports per account at 20 per transaction (my arithmetic). A pre-reduction token account frees 550,840 lamports at step 2 and 1,835,352 in total after step 5. Sweeping after each step collects the excess as it appears. Waiting until step 5 collects it in one pass. An early sweep forfeits nothing, because each later step creates new excess.

Reclaiming early forfeits nothing: each later step over-funds the account again, and the excess has no deadline. The only cost of reclaiming is the base fee per transaction. Sweeping after each step collects the excess as it appears; waiting for step 5 collects it in one pass. Raydium adds that a frozen token account still qualifies, because freezing restricts token movement, not lamports.

Jupiter says its routing sidelines or penalizes sources that underdeliver: the routing docs describe a self-learning mechanism that sidelines underperforming sources, and trade press on Metis V8 reports slippage penalties on venues with poor realized execution plus just-in-time onchain split selection. Neither source gives before/after execution data.
The Ultra Swap API is marked no longer actively maintained and superseded by Swap V2. Older Jupiter pages still cite stale defaults, so pin to the current developer docs when quoting fee numbers.

On a dynamic-fee pool the fee a quote returns can change between block N and block N+1 even if reserves have not moved, because every swap shifts the volatility accumulator; Raydium says a quote can be off by a few bps if a reactive pool is hit between quote and execution, and that the accumulator and last-update timestamp are public on-chain so clients can replicate the formula. Meteora's design behaves the same way: the accumulator rises with bin movement and decays with elapsed time.

On /order, Metis (Jupiter's on-chain multi-hop, multi-split router), JupiterZ (off-chain RFQ market makers), Dflow and OKX compete on every request and the best execution price wins; Jupiter says a self-learning mechanism sidelines underperforming sources. Optional parameters can shrink the field: a receiver or a payer different from the taker removes Dflow and OKX, excludeRouters=jupiterz removes JupiterZ, and referral parameters leave all four eligible. Jupiter's v6 aggregator program added a positive slippage fee, audited by Offside Labs between Aug 1 and Oct 2, 2025. When the result beats the quote, the program can charge a share (positive_slippage_bps) of the excess to a fee account: output above quoted_out_amount on exact-in routes, input below quoted_in_amount on exact-out routes. The report does not say which Jupiter products or routes enable the fee, and the Swap V2 pages read for this pass do not mention it.

Offside Labs' Oct 2025 audit of Jupiter Aggregator v6 found 0 critical, 2 high, 1 medium, 0 low and 1 informational issue, all high and medium ones fixed. High: on exact-out routes the positive slippage fee fell as positive slippage grew beyond quoted_in_amount x positive_slippage_bps and was discontinuous at that point. High: on exact-in routes the fee could exceed the positive slippage (worked example: quote 100, received 121, rate 0.2 gives fee 24 on a gain of 21, so the user receives 97, less than the quote), fixed in commit 20af53e. Superseded Jupiter pages stay online and rank in search. The Ultra fees page and the Metis common-errors page carry notices that those APIs are 'no longer actively maintained' and superseded by Swap V2, while the Mar 31, 2026 changelog says Ultra and Metis APIs 'remain available'. The Oct 2025 Ultra V3 post names routers (Iris, Hashflow) that the 2026 docs do not list. Quote fee numbers from the current Swap V2 pages and re-check them, because the older pages still show the same bps table but may drift.

On /order, the top-level feeBps field is the total fee rate and platformFee.feeBps is Jupiter's platform fee alone. The two differ when a gasless surcharge applies. feeMint names the token the fee is taken in, chosen from a priority list: SOL, stablecoins, liquid staking tokens, bluechips, others. After /execute, the fee equals totalInputAmount minus inputAmountResult when feeMint is the input mint, or outputAmountResult minus totalOutputAmount when it is the output mint.

The /build (Router) path charges no Jupiter swap fee and routes through Metis only. An integrator can add its own fee with platformFeeBps and a feeAccount, which can be any SPL token account it controls. /build uses a fixed 50 bps slippage by default and switches to RTSE only when the caller passes slippageBps=rtse.

A tip is only paid when the bundle lands. Jito's docs say that if the tip is in the same transaction as the strategy and that transaction fails, you do not pay the tip. A losing or expired bundle therefore costs no tip, but it still costs searcher infrastructure. A DEV Community post claims the opposite model (refund only on ingress rejection) without citing a source.

Whether a lost bundle still costs a tip is disputed. Jito's docs say bundles are all-or-nothing and a failed bundle is rolled back entirely, which implies a tip inside it does not commit. RPC Fast says the tip is still paid when a bundle reverts on chain, and a DEV post says a submitted but outcompeted bundle still pays. No primary Jito source addresses refunds. Test on chain before budgeting for failed-bundle tips.

A tip moves only if the bundle lands, because it is a transfer inside the bundle. Jito's docs advise putting the tip in the same transaction as the strategy so that, if that transaction fails, you do not pay the tip. By atomicity, a bundle that loses the auction or expires never executes and so pays no tip (an inference from the bundle rules, not a sentence in the docs). Jito's FullSend page states the same conditional rule for its own tip: if the transaction fails, the tip is not transferred.

Ghost describes three kinds of wide sandwich. 'Toxic' attacks target specific victim transactions. 'Momentum' attacks ride expected flow and may or may not have seen the victim transaction. 'Launch bots' buy a new token and pool in a bundle and sell quickly, not based on seeing victim transactions. The top wide-sandwich bot sends two bundles when it sees a target: one with the frontrun, one with the victim plus a first backrun that sells enough to break even; a second backrun aims to land one block later. Top bots wait for high-value victims and average about 0.46 SOL per sandwich.

Jupiter's JLP markets (SOL, ETH, wBTC) charge no funding rate. A trader pays a borrow fee on the full position size for as long as the position is open. The fee accrues without compounding and is settled from collateral when the position changes or closes.

On Jupiter's JLP markets every position pays a borrow fee and none receives funding. Gauntlet wrote in May 2024 that Jupiter's mechanism exchanges capital between traders and JLP holders, not between longs and shorts. Chaos Labs wrote in February 2025 that Jupiter lacks a true funding-rate mechanism, which limits its use for long-lived short hedges.

Holding costs eat margin. Pacifica deducts funding from an isolated position's margin balance and recalculates its liquidation price after each payout. Jupiter's accrued borrow fees count against collateral, so the liquidation price drifts toward the market even when the position is untouched.

Interventions against Solana sandwiching, in order: Jito suspended its mempool (announced 8 March 2024); the Solana Foundation removed operators from its delegation program (10 June 2024); Marinade's MIP-9 blocklisted 73 validators from its stake auction (proposed 7 February 2025); Jito's JIP-15 blacklist was reported executed in a 7 May 2025 update; the JIP-22 mechanism blacklisted 28 validators in its first wave (update of 17 September 2025). The arXiv study uses the mempool closure, the Foundation removal, MIP-9 and an October 2025 JitoSOL delisting as its era boundaries.

The arXiv study (Heimbach et al., 23 September 2026) counts 28.0 million sandwiches on Solana, against 38,567 on Tron, 30,607 on Ethereum and 1,889 on Base. It treats Solana as 'protected order flow' because there is no public mempool. Its five eras start in July 2023, March 2024, June 2024, February 2025 and October 2025. They hold 2.3M, 2.6M, 11.1M, 6.7M and 5.2M sandwiches, at about 9,000, 28,000, 46,000, 26,000 and 20,000 per day.

When Velocity's longs and shorts are unbalanced, its AMM takes the other side of the leftover. Rent minimums should be read from the getMinimumBalanceForRentExemption RPC (or the Rent sysvar), never hardcoded, because the rate changes with each SIMD-0437 step. Local solana-test-validator 4.3.0 still starts at 6,960 lamports per byte, so reclaim logic should be tested on Devnet.

WithdrawExcessLamports rejects native (wrapped SOL) token accounts with NativeNotSupported, because their lamport balance is their token balance. To recover a wrapped SOL account's rent, close it (balance and rent both return) or use UnwrapLamports (discriminator 45), which unwraps all or a set amount without closing the account. The owner signs, or a delegate up to its delegated amount.

Raydium says it added admin instructions to return rent held by its pool vaults and state accounts: AMM v4 WithdrawExcessLamports (tag 18) and CPMM and LaunchLab CollectExcessLamports on 2026-09-09, and CLMM CollectExcessLamports on 2026-09-30. Stable AMM has none. The sweep moves lamports only, so token balances and swap quotes are unchanged, and a CLMM position's own rent still returns only when the position is closed.

Two safeguards cover a rent increase. The SIMD-0438 reset gate (set_lamports_per_byte_to_6960) can raise the rate back to 6,960 for new allocations. SIMD-0392 (Activated; Chainstack gives mainnet slot 443,664,000) changes the post-execution floor to min(rent minimum, pre-execution balance) when an account has a balance, does not grow and keeps its owner. An account that already withdrew its excess therefore stays usable after a reset, unless it grows, changes owner or loses lamports below its starting balance.

Raydium added admin sweep instructions for rent held by its pools: WithdrawExcessLamports (tag 18) on AMM v4 on 2026-09-09, and CollectExcessLamports on CPMM, LaunchLab and (from 2026-09-30) CLMM. Each is signed by the program admin or a dedicated collect-lamports wallet. Raydium says this rent belongs to the protocol, not to LPs, and that the sweeps move only lamports. Rent for a CLMM position returns only when the position closes, and the LaunchLab base mint's rent is stranded because its mint authority is revoked.

Half of the base fee is burned and the other half goes to the block leader. Since SIMD-0096 (status Activated) the leader also receives 100% of the priority fee, so validator reward = base_fee/2 + prioritization_fee. Before SIMD-0096 the priority fee was also split 50/50 burn/leader.

SIMD-0096 drawback recorded in the SIMD itself: because the leader keeps 100% of priority fees, a leader can inflate the priority fees reported in its own blocks at minimal cost, which can lead wallets to overestimate the fee they need.

Agave's calculate_reward_and_burn_fee_details burns transaction_fee x 50 / 100 and deposits priority_fee + (transaction_fee - burn) to the leader, so the leader gets 100% of the priority fee and half of the base fee. The 50% is a static constant (DEFAULT_BURN_PERCENT); Firedancer hard-codes FD_PACK_TXN_FEE_BURN_PCT = 50. SIMD-0096 (status Activated) is the change that stopped burning half of the priority fee.

SIMD-0096's own Drawbacks section notes that because the leader keeps 100% of the priority fee, a leader can inflate the priority fees reported in its own blocks at minimal cost, which may lead wallets to overestimate the fee they need.

Scheduler cost constants, in CUs: signature 720; Secp256k1 verify 6,690; Ed25519 strict verify 2,400; Secp256r1 verify 4,800; write lock 300 per writable account; instruction data 1 CU per 4 bytes. In early 2024 (March, per Helius) Jito discontinued its mempool stream. It gave searchers a roughly 200 ms preview of pending transactions, and searchers used it for sandwich attacks. Jito gave up revenue to stop it.

Bundles exist to stop spam. Umbra (2023) said about 96% of attempted atomic arbitrages on Solana failed and filled blocks with failed transactions. RPC Fast, citing internal Jito research, says over 60% of block compute in a typical 2022 epoch went to arbitrage attempts, over 98% of which failed. Failed bundles never land on chain.

Jito's Block Engine ran a mempool that held each transaction up to 200 ms so searchers could see it. Solana has no public mempool. Transactions are forwarded to upcoming leaders, which limits pre-inclusion visibility but does not remove it. Early Solana studies found no sandwiching. Chorus One's May 2022 sample of 12,106 Orca swaps over about 5 hours (922 of 1,696 validators as leaders, 54.37%) found no evidence of sandwich attacks and argued that without a mempool only leaders (and possibly RPCs) could profit. Raydium separates price impact from slippage and tolerance. Price impact, impact = (p_before - p_after) / p_before, is a deterministic property of a trade against a specific pool state and can be computed before submission (about 2 x amount_in / reserve_in for small constant-product trades; piecewise on CLMM pools). Realized slippage is (quoted_out - actual_out) / quoted_out. Tolerance is a buffer around the impact: minAmountOut = amountOut x (1 - tolerance), so a 2% impact with 0.5% tolerance puts the floor about 2.5% below pre-trade spot.

Holding costs are charged on notional but paid from margin, so they erode liquidation distance. GUM adds or takes funding from account value. Pacifica deducts funding from isolated margin and recalculates liquidation prices after every payout. Jupiter says borrow fees count against collateral and move the liquidation price closer. Phoenix counts pending funding in account health in real time. Read a quoted rate against margin by multiplying by leverage: 0.00125% per hour of notional is 0.025% per hour of margin at 20x, about 0.6% per day (derived).

Makers are not paid on most Solana perp venues. GUM says its maker fee 'is a charge, not a rebate'; Jupiter Beta and Phoenix charge makers 0.5 bps; Pacifica charges makers 0.015% at base and 0.000% only from VIP 1 ($100M in 14 days). Velocity is the exception: a flat 0.25 bps rebate to post-only makers, paid out of the taker fee.

Jupiter's borrow fee against other venues' funding steers flow. In Feb 2025 SOL utilization fell to an all-time low near 30% while Jupiter charged ~30% APR and other venues' funding was low or negative (forum author DimOK). Chaos Labs reports the opposite regime after the Nov 2024 US election: utilization sat at 100% for weeks with SOL rates at their maximum (~90% in its chart), and it argues volume rises in volatile periods regardless of rates. Both accounts agree utilization responds to the gap between the borrow fee and what funding venues charge.

Cost parameters move, so every number needs a date. Jupiter's open/close fee was 10 bps when Gauntlet recommended 7 bps on 2024-05-03; the Nov 2026 docs list 6 bps. The borrow model went from a single linear curve (hourly rate = utilization x max hourly rate, with 0.01% per hour = 88% APR as the old cap) to a jump-rate proposal on 2024-05-21 and a dual-slope recommendation on 2024-12-19. Velocity calls its fee and funding values admin-settable, Jupiter says the Beta engine can adjust fees, and Phoenix can change its Tailwind rebate from the next rewards day.

Liquidation is a fee event, not only a close. On Jupiter JLP markets all remaining collateral is taken as the liquidation fee after the loss, close fee and borrow fees. On Beta markets the forced close pays the 0.035% taker fee plus a liquidation fee of 0.75% (crypto) or 1% (stock markets) and what remains is returned, which in a fast market can be little or nothing. GUM charges each liquidation close the taker fee plus a liquidation fee, never more than the sub-account holds.

Sandwiches concentrate on newly launched, illiquid memecoins. Bitquery found Pump.fun's launch curve and PumpSwap account for 96% of 6.85M attacks detected between 30 Oct 2025 and 7 Oct 2026. Helius found 16 of the 20 most-sandwiched tokens in 7 Dec 2024 to 5 Jan 2025 were Pump.fun tokens. Ghost says buys of new low-cap tokens are the likeliest targets because of thin liquidity, high default slippage and speed-first traders.

Victims are mostly traders who accept high slippage on thin-liquidity tokens, often through Telegram bots and memecoin apps. Helius says memecoin traders set high slippage to land fast and favour Telegram bots. Marinade says attacks 'primarily target high-slippage trades from Telegram trading bots'. Ghost found that buys of new low-cap tokens are the most likely wide-sandwich targets (low liquidity, high default slippage, speed over price). Bitquery found 96% of detected attacks on Pump.fun's launch curve and PumpSwap.

Cost-model rule for a held perp position: JLP-market cost is the open and close fees plus price impact plus the borrow fee times hours open (about $0.16/hour per $10,000 at the docs' illustrative 0.0016%/hour). A funding venue's cost is the maker or taker fees plus signed funding, which can be a credit. Compare them over the intended holding time, not by headline fee alone.

In the arXiv study, daily Solana sandwich volume peaked above 100,000 per day (around Feb 2024, Jito mempool era), later reached about 46,000 per day and settled near 20,000 per day. Over the same eras the share of sandwiches landing in slots led by over-represented validators fell from 50% to 2%. So validator blacklists cut one exposure signal while attack volume stayed high.

Stake-pool blacklists use explicit sandwich-rate thresholds. Marinade's policy blacklists a validator that sandwiches in over 30% of the blocks it produces and charges a one-time bond penalty. Jito's JIP-22 flags a validator whose sandwich rate exceeds max(25%, 2x cluster median) over 10 consecutive epochs, using Ghost API data. Its first wave blacklisted 28 validators. The arXiv study dates the Marinade blocklist to Feb 2025 and the JitoSOL delisting to Oct 2025.

Jito suspended its public mempool in March 2024 after its ~200 ms preview of pending transactions was heavily used for sandwiching. Heimbach et al. measured more than 100,000 sandwiches per day around February 2024 and an abrupt drop at the closure. They saw no considerable Solana sandwiching before late 2023 (first protected-flow attack on 16 Aug 2023).

Sandwiching moved into validator- and relay-operated private mempools after the closure. The Solana Foundation removed a group of operators from its delegation program (SFDP) on 10 Jun 2024 for participating in mempools that allow sandwich attacks. Helius (Jan 2025) described DeezNode's private mempool and validators receiving profit-share offers to join private mempools. JIP-15 (4 Mar 2025) cited roughly 14% of Jito Stake Pool validators as engaged in private mempool participation.

Stake-pool rules are built on a per-validator 'sandwich rate': Ghost defines it as the share of a validator's blocks containing at least one sandwich over 30 days (cluster average about 5%, outliers 30-60%, per AI-generated notes of its May 2025 talk). Jito's trigger is 25% (or twice the cluster median) over 10 epochs; Marinade's is over 30% of blocks produced.

Jito's pool (JitoSOL) used staged blacklists. JIP-4 (a 2024 DAO vote) removed validators for private-mempool participation. JIP-15 (proposed 4 March 2025) set up a working group to review an investigation finding about 14% of Jito stake pool validators in private mempools. A 7 May 2025 update reports the blacklist was executed with a slightly reduced list, a 50-epoch removal and no appeals process. A commenter put 2.4M SOL (about 15% of the pool) on the flagged validators. JIP-22 (18 July 2025) then replaced one-off votes with an epoch rule: flag a validator whose sandwich rate over 10 consecu

Heimbach et al. find validator-level concentration of sandwiches faded as stake programs delisted validators. The share of attacks landing in slots of over-represented leaders fell from 50% in the Jito-mempool era to 2% in the final era. The ten most over-represented leaders' excess fell from 1.68x to 1.01x by the Marinade era, and only 6 leaders were under- and 8 over-represented in the final era. Victim concentration moved to specific trading apps.

The Helius Solana MEV Report (Jan 2025) says Jito internal analysis traces just under half of Solana sandwiches to one program, DeezNode's 'Vpe' bot, which operates through a private mempool. Over Dec 7 2024 to Jan 5 2025 it ran 1.55M sandwiches at 88.9% success and earned 65,880 SOL (about $13.43M), roughly 0.0425 SOL per attack. Figures are gross and from a single report.

Velocity funding (docs.drift.trade now redirects to docs.velocity.exchange) is hourly and based on (market TWAP - oracle TWAP) / oracle TWAP / 24, with a floor of oracle TWAP/3333 (about 10.95% annualized), a per-market dead zone, and premium caps of 3%, 5% or 10% of oracle TWAP by market tier. The AMM covers imbalance between sides, capped at one third of its retained equity per period, and the insurance fund does not cover funding shortfalls.

Funding caps differ by venue. Pacifica's docs cap funding at +/-4% per hour (the page footer says it was last updated about a year before 2026-11-06). Hyperliquid caps it at 0.5% per hour. Velocity caps the premium at 3% of the oracle TWAP for contract tiers A and B, 5% for tier C and 10% below that.

Velocity aims to charge longs and shorts the same funding rate, but its AMM takes the leftover imbalance. The AMM may spend at most one third of its retained equity per funding period on asymmetric funding; past that, the paying side's rate is capped and receipts are scaled to what is available. The insurance fund is never drawn on to cover a funding shortfall. The premium is capped at 3% of oracle TWAP for contract tiers A and B, 5% for tier C and 10% below. A per-market dead zone and ramp slope shape the rate between the oracle floor and the cap.

In the Foundation's cohort study, 75.5% of account-creation events closed within the same transaction, and about 5.7% of allocated bytes survived 1 million slots (about 4.7 days). Gross requested account state was about 10 GiB per day (10.23 GiB on 2026-07-11, 84% classic SPL token accounts), while net live state grew about 0.3 GB per day. An arbitrage bot and its helper program dominated the create-and-close pattern. For such flows rent is a temporary lock-up and the real cost is transaction fees. Single study; its Dune queries are linked in the source.

Blacklists are evaded by re-registering. A Marinade forum proposal (May 14, 2025) says flagged operators changed identity addresses and started new validators, and that sandwich attackers hold over 50% of total stake. That 50% figure is the proposer's own assertion citing a community repo, not an audited number. Marinade later adopted continuous blacklisting with bond slashing.

Heimbach et al. (arXiv v1, 23 Sep 2026) count 28,042,725 sandwiches by 8,631 persistent bots on Solana from 1 Jul 2023 to 30 Jun 2026, aimed at transactions meant to be shielded from front-running. Bot gross profit was $383.4M and net $345.2M after fees (fees take 10.0% of gross); 88.0% of attacks were profitable. Single preprint; Crypto Briefing only relays it.

Ghost's trend data: the wide share of sandwiches rose from 5% to 93% by Oct 2025 (its May 2025 talk put wide at about 30%, up from about 1%). Wide-sandwich extraction peaked at 87,000 SOL in Jan 2025, then held at 30-60k SOL a month. In May 2025 Ghost put all sandwich extraction at $370-500M over 16 months (low end SOL only, high end adds atomic memecoin revenue). The talk page is AI-generated notes and may be inaccurate.

Detector design drives totals. A Jan 2026 preprint on Ethereum rollups (not Solana) found that naive heuristics overstate sandwiching, with most flagged patterns false positives and a negative median net return. Heimbach et al. built their persistence filter for the same reason: a bot that trades both ways a million times with under 1% sandwich-shaped matches is more likely high-frequency trading than an attacker.

Sandwiching on Solana was not always a problem. A Chorus One analysis of about five hours of Orca swaps (12,106 swaps on 14 March 2022) found no evidence of sandwich attacks: 1% of swaps were surrounded by the same user, none in the same block, and the amounts were too small to profit. The three-year arXiv study, whose window starts in July 2023, sees its first notable attack volume in October 2023.

A Ghost (GhostLogs) talk at Accelerate 2025 reported that sandwich bots extracted between $370 million and $500 million from January 2024 to May 2025, measured over about 8.5 billion trades. The lower bound is the USD value of SOL taken. The upper bound adds atomic memecoin revenue. The source is a Solana Compass page whose notes say they are AI generated and may not be 100% accurate, so treat the figures as unverified until checked against the video.

Sandwich profit feeds stake competition. Marinade says sandwiching validators 'can afford to bid higher in staking auctions because of their predatory profits', which crowds out honest validators. Helius's report notes the same criticism of Marinade's auction and tracks a DeezNode validator whose stake rose from 307.9k SOL (13 November, epoch 697) to 802.5k SOL (9 December, epoch 709), with 19.89% of it from Marinade. A Marinade forum critic goes further and says auction bids can only be funded by sandwich attacks; that is an opinion with no measurement behind it.

Marinade's MIP-9 (posted 7 February 2025) blocked 73 validators from receiving auction stake. It flagged validators with public tools when they facilitated 'more than a decent number of sandwich attacks' relative to their stake across multiple epochs. Flagged validators could appeal, with reinstatement after a one-month observation. Hanabi Staking replied that it had found more malicious validators holding over 50% of Marinade stake (provisional, unpublished) and that it is 'very easy to switch keypairs'. Pacifica's base tier charges 0.015% maker and 0.040% taker, falling by tier on 14-day rolling volume. VIP 1 ($100M) has 0% maker and 0.030% taker. VIP 3 ($500M) has 0% maker and 0.028% taker.

Pacifica funding is sampled every 5 seconds and the average is applied hourly. The rate is the premium index plus a clamped adjustment toward a fixed 0.01% interest rate, divided by 8. It is capped at plus or minus 4% per hour. Positive funding means longs pay shorts.

A JLP-market liquidation takes all remaining collateral after the loss, the close fee and the borrow fees. A Beta-market liquidation instead charges a 0.75% to 1% fee on position value (the liquidation price also allows for the 0.035% taker fee) and returns whatever collateral remains, which in a fast market can be little or nothing.

Pacifica's funding formula has the same shape as Hyperliquid's: funding rate = (premium index + clamp(interest rate - premium index, -0.05%, 0.05%)) / 8, with the interest rate fixed at 0.01% per 8 hours. The premium index compares an impact price with the oracle price (Pacifica's impact notional is $20,000 for BTC and $6,000 for other markets). Both venues sample every 5 seconds and apply the hourly average.

On Velocity a borrow is a withdrawal past a zero balance, and the borrow rate depends only on that spot market's utilization. Four admin-set parameters shape the curve: optimal utilization U* (always below 85%), the rate at U*, the rate at 100%, and a minimum rate. Above U* the remaining rate budget splits across six fixed segments (to 85%, 90%, 95%, 99%, 99.5% and 100% utilization) weighted 5/10/15/20/25/25%. Drift v2's program constants carry the same boundaries and weights.
Pacifica's published base tier charges 0.015% maker and 0.040% taker. QuickNode's Pacifica profile states the same as 'around 0.015% and 0.04%'.

Pacifica's tiers fall with 14-day volume: above $5M 0.012% maker / 0.038% taker; above $10M 0.009% / 0.036%; above $25M 0.006% / 0.034%; above $50M 0.003% / 0.032%; VIP 1 to 3 (above $100M, $250M, $500M) 0% maker and 0.030% / 0.029% / 0.028% taker. The page footer says it was last updated about six months before 2026-11-06.

Velocity divides each taker fee in a fixed order. The referee discount, filler (keeper) reward, referrer reward and maker rebate come off first. The remainder splits 15% to the AMM, 15% to the insurance fund and 70% to the protocol on mainnet's live configuration; both shares are admin-settable. Spot fills and direct swaps charge no trading fee.

On Velocity, a fill can cost more than the tier number for traceable reasons. A market can be priced above the schedule (a market 1.5 bps above a 5 bps tier costs 6.5 bps), and a builder fee (capped at 1% of notional) is charged on top of the taker fee. Both are set onchain and readable.

An independent critic argues crypto perp funding is a persistent transfer, not an arbitrage price. Falkenstein (2023-03-17) says funding averaged at least 15% a year, that the modal daily rate was 0.03% (about 11% annualized), and that rates follow recent returns. That 0.03% a day equals the fixed baseline Hyperliquid, Pacifica and Velocity document. His claim of insider manipulation is opinion without audited evidence.

Pacifica's order fees fall by tier on 14-day rolling volume (tiers update daily; subaccounts share the master account's tier). Tier 1 (no volume) is 0.015% maker / 0.040% taker. Tiers 2 to 5 step down 0.003% maker and 0.002% taker each, reaching 0.003% / 0.032% above $50M. VIP 1 (above $100M) is 0.000% / 0.030% and VIP 3 (above $500M) is 0.000% / 0.028%. Makers therefore pay a fee on every tier below VIP 1. The fee page showed 'last updated 6 months ago' at snapshot.

Velocity (the rebuilt Drift) charges takers by trailing 30-day volume, in USDT, applied to the position's cost basis: Regular (under $5M) 6 bps (0.060%), VIP 1 ($5M to $80M) 5 bps, VIP 2 ($80M to $200M) 4 bps, VIP 3 (above $200M) 2 bps. A post-only maker earns a flat 0.25 bps rebate at every tier, paid out of the taker's fee. The table is the baseline for SOL, BTC and ETH perps; other markets can price above or below it, and every rate is admin-settable. Spot fills and direct swaps charge no trading fee. Worked example in the docs: 6 bps on a $2,000 fill is $1.20, so a round trip costs $2.40.

Phoenix funding: F is an 8-hour rate built from the hourly-averaged premium; each hour pays position size x index price x F/8, capped per hour by a per-market maximum funding rate. The clamp radius R and multiplier m depend on market type: crypto R 0.05%, m 1; equities, ETFs and commodities R 0.03%, m 0.5; the pre-IPO market R 0.03%, m 0.125. So the zero-premium baseline for non-crypto Phoenix markets is scaled down (0.5 x 0.01% per 8 hours for stocks and commodities). The per-market cap lives on a Market Parameters page whose snapshot holds no text.

Phoenix 'Tailwind Rewards' return 10% of the funding a trader pays on eligible perp markets, starting 2026-11-04 at 18:00 UTC and running until further notice. The rebate is computed per hourly settlement in which the trader pays; funding received is never netted against it. There is no minimum or cap, every account is eligible, and rebates are claimable within 24 hours after each rewards day (18:00 UTC to 18:00 UTC) as USDC in the cross-margin balance. Phoenix may change the percentage or the market list from the next rewards day.

Pacifica samples its funding rate every 5 seconds, applies the hourly average at the end of each hour, and caps funding at plus or minus 4% per hour. For isolated positions the payment comes out of the isolated margin and liquidation prices are recalculated after every payout. Hyperliquid documents the same formula but a cap of 0.5% per hour, one eighth of Pacifica's. A 4% per hour charge on notional is 80% of margin per hour at 20x leverage (derived), so the cap bounds the worst-case holding cost.

Velocity prices spot borrowing with one utilization curve: a straight line from zero to an optimal utilization point U*, then six steeper segments to 100% that take 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 25% of the rate budget (R_max minus R_opt). Admins set U*, R_opt, R_max and R_min per market. The docs' illustrative market (U* 80%, R_opt 10%, R_max 50% APR) charges 12% at 85% utilization and 30% at 99%. Borrowing is a withdrawal past a zero balance, has no term, and interest compounds through a borrow index in the borrowed asset. Pacifica's money market charges USDC borrowers interest that accrues every 60 seconds (pending_interest += required_borrow x borrow_rate_per_second x 60), is charged to the borrower's USDC balance hourly and is paid pro rata to lenders; APR is compounded per second. The borrow curve runs linearly from MIN_BORROW_APR 1% to LINEAR_KINK_APR 10.95% at 80% utilization, then exponentially toward EXPONENTIAL_TARGET_APR 50% at 100%. Lender APR = borrow APR x utilization. The page carries no date.

On a funding venue the quiet-market default is that longs pay: Hyperliquid's SOL, BTC and ETH funding all read +10.95% annualized on 2025-01-30, consistent with the premium sitting inside the clamp band so that only the baseline interest term applied (an inference from the identical readings). Falkenblog (2023) reports the modal daily funding rate in crypto perps as 0.03% (about 11% annualized). Budget roughly 11% APR on a long when the perp tracks the oracle and more when it trades at a premium; negative readings do occur (Drift BTC-PERP was -10.87% that day).

Press fee figures for Velocity conflict with the venue docs. A Tron Weekly article republished by edgeX (2026-08-25, citing a SolanaFloor tweet about the private beta) gives 0.01% in its summary and 0.02% in its headline and body. Velocity's docs list a 6 bps (0.060%) taker fee at the Regular tier and 2 bps (0.020%) only above $200M of trailing 30-day volume. Prefer the venue's live fee table over launch coverage.

In the Foundation's cohort, 75.5% of account-creation events close in the same transaction, and 5.65% of the initially allocated bytes remain after 1 million slots (about 4.7 days). Trading flows create and close token accounts inside one transaction, so the deposit is borrowed, not spent: the cost is temporary capital plus fees. The Foundation study names an arbitrage bot that uses a helper program to create and close accounts, and finds the live footprint of both addresses small (about 0.46 GB and 0.0008 GB). Turnkey's example is a swap that wraps SOL into a temporary wrapped-SOL account, uses it and closes it before the transaction ends.

Third-party cleanup tools take a cut or claim not to. Sol Incinerator is described as charging about 2% of reclaimed rent for closing empty token accounts; a Jumpbit guide claims 0% fees in single-wallet mode. Both figures come from listings and vendor guides, not the tools' own terms.

The Foundation's model puts the capital for a state-bloat attack at about $17.2M after a tenfold rent cut ($50,000 per GB target x 343 GB of live-state headroom), or $51M if validators run 2 TB. Inputs: $0.50 per GB disk, 1,000 validators, a 100x safety multiplier. The authors call it a capital requirement, not a guaranteed loss, because rent is recoverable on close. They say the model ignores external attacker payoffs and that their correlations are not a causal estimate of rent elasticity. The author works for the Foundation, which backs the cut.

Third-party closers charge for the refund. Sol Incinerator takes about 2% of reclaimed rent for standard empty-account closes and about 5% for NFT burns, and its listing says competitors charge 5% to 20%. A Jumpbit guide claims no tool fee beyond network fees. Both sources are vendor-written. A direct CloseAccount costs only the network fee.

Third-party cleaners take a cut that varies. Streamflow's Dust Collector documents 0.000102 SOL per closed account, stated as 5% of the rent (page dated 2026-04-17). It skips frozen accounts, and its value slider can burn tokens that still have a balance. A Compass listing says Sol Incinerator takes about 2% for empty-account closures and about 5% for NFT burns, and that rivals charge 5% to 20%; those figures are third-party copy, not the tools' own terms. Jumpbit's own post says its cleaner charges only network costs. Binance.US lists no extra fee for its wallet feature.

Never hardcode rent. Read the minimum with getMinimumBalanceForRentExemption in clients or Rent::get()?.minimum_balance in programs. getMinimumBalanceForRentExemption(0) equals 128 x lamports_per_byte, so dividing by 128 shows the active step (650,240 / 128 = 5,080 on 2026-11-06). Raydium notes that the Rent sysvar now carries lamports_per_byte_year with exemption_threshold = 1.0 (SIMD-0194), so do not multiply the fields yourself.

If SIMD-0553 activates, the fee becomes base inclusion fee + priority fee + resource fee. The inclusion fee is a flat 2,500 lamports per transaction, paid wholly to the leader, replacing 5,000 per signature. The resource fee is 100% burned: ceil(requested_cost_units x rate), with the rate stepping 1/10, 1/4, then 1/2 lamport per cost unit through three feature gates. Requested cost units sum signature, write-lock, instruction-data, requested CU limit and requested loaded-data costs. Priority fees do not change. The Foundation analysis calls the governance proposal SGP-0003.

Priority fee = ceil(compute_unit_price x compute_unit_limit / 1,000,000) lamports, with the price in micro-lamports per CU. The default price is 0, so a transaction with no SetComputeUnitPrice pays no priority fee. The division rounds up: live probes on 2026-11-06 gave +1 lamport for price 1 x limit 1 and +2 lamports for price 1 x limit 1,000,001. The product saturates: price u64::MAX x limit 1,400,000 returned a total fee of u64::MAX (18,446,744,073,709,551,615). Agave 1.18.8 unit tests pin the same rounding and saturation.

Unit mistakes are expensive. SetComputeUnitPrice is in micro-lamports per CU, not lamports: price 1,000,000,000,000 with a 200,000-CU limit priced a total fee of 200,000,005,000 lamports (about 200 SOL) in a live getFeeForMessage probe. In v1 the priority fee is a total in lamports, so applying price x limit / 1,000,000 to priorityFee is also wrong.

The scheduler ranks transactions by priority = reward x 1,000,000 / (cost + 1). Reward is the priority fee plus the non-burned half of the base fee. Cost is the scheduler's estimate: signature cost + write-lock cost + instruction-data cost + the requested CU limit (programs execution cost) + loaded-accounts data cost. Agave's own comment says the +1 only avoids division by zero.

Bundles that touch disjoint accounts, or only read the same accounts (r,r), run in separate auctions. Within an auction, bundles are ordered by requested tip per requested compute unit, and Jito submits the highest-paying combination to the validator up to a compute-unit limit. Priority fee = ceil(compute_unit_price x compute_unit_limit / 1,000,000) lamports, where the price is in micro-lamports per CU. Block packing reserves a transaction's estimated cost, which is based on the requested CU limit, in CostTracker::try_add and later calls update_cost to replace it with the actual cost after execution; the tracker documents in-flight transactions as 'waiting for an update with actual usage'. So an oversized limit costs block capacity only while the transaction is in flight, but the lamport priority fee is fixed by the requested limit and is not adjusted.

SIMD-0553 would make a loose CU limit costly even with no priority fee, because the resource fee is charged on the requested limit. Recommendations differ: 10% (Solana docs, Anza), 10-20% (Chainstack, Metaplex), about 25% (Raydium), and a fixed buffer of at least 300 CUs in QuickNode's Kit client. Worked example from the formula: the Solana docs' sample sets limit 300,000 and price 1 micro-lamport, so the priority fee is ceil(300,000 x 1 / 1,000,000) = ceil(0.3) = 1 lamport and a one-signature transaction pays 5,001 lamports in total. The cost model charges loaded account data at 8 CUs (DEFAULT_HEAP_COST) per 32 KiB page, rounded up. In v1, an unset or zero loaded-data limit counts as one 32 KiB page.

A Solana sandwich is a front-run buy, the victim's swap, then a back-run sell by the same attacker, with the front-run pushing the price to the edge of the victim's slippage limit. The classic form is an atomic three-transaction Jito bundle in which transactions 1 and 3 share a signer and transaction 2 is signed by someone else.

Bundle protection can fail on uncled blocks. A Jito bundle is a list of up to 5 fully signed transactions that execute in the listed order, atomically and all-or-nothing, inside one slot. A bundle cannot cross a slot boundary. The same account list can give different numbers, because providers combine accounts differently. Agave's stock method starts from the block minimum and takes the maximum with each supplied account's minimum. Triton takes the requested percentile over the transactions that write-lock each account and returns the highest of those values. Helius's Atlas code has two variants: v1 pools the transactions of all requested accounts into one group, and v2 keeps one group per account. Both then take the higher of the account-level and network-wide percentile at each level. Chainstack and OrbitFlare bot

IMC 2025 (Northeastern Univ.) measured sandwiches visible in Jito bundles over about four months in early 2025: 521,903 attacks costing victims over $7.7M, with only 0.038% of all measured Jito bundles being sandwiches. The authors call sandwiching 'relatively rare overall' in that slice. Scope limit: the method only sees three-transaction Jito bundles, so it misses sandwiches that bypass Jito.

Every published count comes from a heuristic detector, so treat counts as method-dependent. Gerzon et al. inspect only length-3 Jito bundles (2.77% of daily bundles), miss disguised sandwiches, and leave the 28% of attacks with no SOL leg out of dollar totals. Heimbach et al. add a persistence filter (bots with at least 100 sandwiches, 60% profitable) and note 36.0% of Solana sandwiches enclose more than one victim. Bitquery warns chain data cannot prove the bot saw the order and some flagged wallets may be fast traders.

A Jito bundle holds at most 5 transactions. They execute sequentially and atomically within a single slot: if any transaction fails, none commit, and a bundle cannot cross a slot boundary. Bundles are only forwarded to leaders running Jito-Solana.

Users report the sendBundle error 'Bundle Dropped, no connected leader up soon'. Read literally, the Block Engine saw no connected Jito leader scheduled soon. Jito warns that tips do not prioritize transactions at validators that are not Jito-Solana leaders, so a tip aimed at such a slot is wasted. Jito's GitBook adds that bundles are not forwarded between validators.

Uncled-block risk: when a leader's block is skipped (an 'uncled block'), any party that received it can rebroadcast its transactions through the normal banking stage. That stage does not enforce bundle atomicity or revert protection, so transactions from a bundle can land alone and revert on-chain. Jito's mitigations are pre/post account checks and the tip inside the strategy transaction. Jito says it never explicitly leaks bundles, but uncled blocks expose them. No independent incident write-up of an 'uncle bandit' loss was found.

The tip is the bid. It is a SOL transfer, as a top-level or CPI instruction in any transaction of the bundle, to one of 8 fixed Jito tip accounts returned by getTipAccounts. Block Engine bundles must tip at least 1,000 lamports; below that, clients see the error 'Bundle must tip at least 1000 lamports'. Jito advises choosing a tip account at random to reduce contention.

Helius 'MEV Protect' is an opt-in routing feature: add mev-protect=true to the endpoint URL (off by default). Helius sends the transaction while avoiding leaders whose own blocks or adjacent blocks repeatedly include sandwiches, but only when the pattern is statistically significant. That excludes roughly 3-4 million SOL of stake at any time. It works with sendTransaction, sendBundle, Sender Max and Sender SWQOS-only. It does not change the tip or priority-fee requirement, can slightly lower the inclusion rate, and Helius advises measuring inclusion with and without it. It lowers risk; it does

A sandwich needs early sight of the victim's pending swap. The attacker buys first and pushes the price up. The victim fills at a worse price, within their slippage limit. The attacker then sells into that price. Solana has no public mempool: transactions go to the upcoming leader, and unprocessed ones expire after about 150 blocks (about one minute). That narrows the window but does not close it. Attackers get sight through validators that share order flow, private mempools, or unprotected submission paths.

If execution exceeds the CU limit the runtime aborts with ComputationalBudgetExceeded (VM message 'exceeded maximum number of instructions allowed (N) at instruction #M'), and the fee is still charged because fees are deducted from the fee payer before execution.

The VM error text 'exceeded maximum number of instructions allowed ({1}) at instruction #{0}' refers to sBPF instructions, not transaction instructions, and #{0} is the index where the limit was hit, not a consumption count. rbpf issue #452 (closed 2023-04-04 via PR #455) records the confusion; the repo was archived 2025-01-10.

SIMD-0182 (Activated): when the sBPF VM fails with any error other than SyscallError (an abort mid-basic-block), the CU meter is fully depleted and the transaction is charged its full requested CU limit; successes and SyscallError failures are charged CUs actually executed. This changes CU accounting (block cost) for irregular failures, and makes an oversized limit costlier on those failures.

SetLoadedAccountsDataSizeLimit (discriminator 4, u32 bytes) caps loaded account data; the default and maximum are 64 MiB. Loaded account data is charged at 8 CU per 32 KB in the scheduler cost model, so the default adds about 16,000 CUs of cost and a smaller explicit limit lowers the cost. Anza's worked table does not reconcile arithmetically.

Block-level CU limits: the Solana docs page (citing Agave v3.1.8) lists MAX_BLOCK_UNITS 60,000,000, MAX_WRITABLE_ACCOUNT_UNITS 12,000,000, MAX_VOTE_UNITS 36,000,000. Solana Compass reports SIMD-0286 raised the block limit to 100M CUs at epoch 1009 on 2026-07-29 (prior step 50M->60M via SIMD-0256, July 2025).

The maximum block size is 100M CUs. SIMD-0286 activated on mainnet on 2026-07-29 at the start of epoch 1009 behind feature gate P1BCUMpAC7V2GRBRiJCNUgpMyWZhoqt3LKo712ePqsz (testnet epoch 983, devnet epoch 1100), after SIMD-0256 raised the limit from 50M to 60M in July 2025. Agave master keeps MAX_BLOCK_UNITS_SIMD_0256 = 60M as the base constant and adds MAX_BLOCK_UNITS_SIMD_0286 = 100M for the activated gate. The per-transaction cap of 1.4M CUs did not change. The Solana docs compute-budget page still lists MAX_BLOCK_UNITS 60,000,000 and calls SIMD-0286 a proposal, so it is stale.

SIMD-0306 (Activated) replaces the static 12M per-account write cap with 40% of the block CU limit: 24M at 60M blocks and 40M at 100M blocks. Agave master sets MAX_WRITABLE_ACCOUNT_UNITS = 24,000,000, and Helius's Agave 3.0 post says the cap rises to 24M and then 40M once SIMD-0286 is active. The Solana docs and the Foundation's 100M-CU page still say 12M, so which value is live is unresolved.

Set the loaded-accounts limit as well as the CU limit. SetLoadedAccountsDataSizeLimit (discriminator 4, u32 bytes, must be above 0) defaults to and is capped at 64 MiB, which adds 16,384 CUs to the scheduler cost. A tighter limit lowers cost and so raises priority for the same fee; Anza and Helius both recommend it.

A transaction that runs out of CUs fails with a VM message of the form 'exceeded maximum number of instructions allowed (N) at instruction #M'. It counts sBPF instructions, not transaction instructions; rbpf issue 452 (opened 2023-03-23) records the confusion, and the rbpf repository was archived on 2025-01-10. Raydium's runbook shows (200000) in the message for a default-sized budget, tells you to run solana confirm <signature> -v to read 'consumed N of M compute units', and says to raise the limit or split the transaction when the 1.4M cap is hit.

The VM error 'exceeded maximum number of instructions allowed (N) at instruction #M' counts sBPF instructions, not transaction instructions. N is the CU limit and #M is the sBPF instruction index where the meter ran out, not a consumption count. rbpf issue #452 records the confusion; it closed on 2023-04-04 through PR #455, and the repository was archived on 2025-01-10. Raydium's guide lists this error as the symptom of CU exhaustion and says to raise the limit or split the transaction.

Solana Foundation data (2026-08-21) shows requests far exceed use: consumed cost units are about 20% of requested on aggregate, and transactions that set both a CU limit and a loaded-data limit over-request about 95k CUs on average (p90 about 280k). 48.6% of transactions set both limits, 43% set only the CU limit, and 8.4% use both defaults. Transactions on defaults over-request the most.

Recommended estimation workflow: simulate to set the compute limit (units consumed plus a 10-20% margin), query fees for the writable accounts, choose a percentile by urgency (median for routine, high for time-critical), multiply price by limit, enforce a hard per-transaction cap, then log the estimated fee, the landed fee and the slot delta to tune from your own data.

Landing and success are different things. Helius (undated, data to Dec 2024) reports that 41.2% of non-vote transactions reverted in Dec 2024 (peak 75.7% in Apr 2024), with bots sending over 100,000 transactions a day accounting for 95.2% of reverts. A transaction that lands can still fail.

In the open-source Atlas code, defaults change depending on whether the request carries an options object. With no options object, vote transactions are included and empty slots are not counted as zero. With an options object that leaves includeVote and evaluateEmptySlotAsZero unset, votes are excluded and empty slots count as zero. When lookbackSlots is omitted, all tracked slots are used. The field comment says 'default 50 ... max 300', but validation enforces 1 to max_lookback_slots (150 by default, error text 'between 1 and 150').

Estimators fed by Geyser or Yellowstone gRPC streams need updated clients to see v1 fees at all. Helius says older Yellowstone protos predate the v1 message fields, so consumers never see transactionConfig, and it lists yellowstone-grpc-client 13.3.0 and yellowstone-grpc-proto 12.6.0 as the first versions with v1 support. Requests for full transaction data that omit maxSupportedTransactionVersion: 1 fail with JSON-RPC error -32015 once they touch a v1 transaction. For getBlock, one v1 transaction anywhere in the block fails the whole request. QuickNode also lists stalled blockSubscribe streams

Headline failure rates count reverts among included transactions, not drops, and they do not condition on fee. Dune data cited in April 2024 showed 75.4% of non-vote transactions failing on 2024-04-04 (the peak). Helius CEO Mert Mumtaz attributed most of that to bots failing arbitrage attempts, a share the report does not quantify. The ISSTA sample has 1,510,834,168 failed of 2,898,175,006 non-vote transactions (about 52%). It reports 58.43% failures for bot accounts and 6.22% for human accounts. Swap V2 has two paths. /order is a meta-aggregator where Metis (onchain multi-hop, multi-split), JupiterZ (off-chain RFQ market makers) and the third-party routers Dflow and OKX all compete and the best execution price wins. /build uses Metis only. JupiterZ transactions cannot be modified after return, so CPI or custom-instruction use cases must use /build.

Slippage is set by the Real-Time Slippage Estimator on /order (from token category, recent slippage data and live failure rates); on /build pass slippageBps=rtse or a fixed number. When realized output falls under the tolerance the swap fails with program error 6001 SlippageToleranceExceeded (fix: raise fixed slippage or use dynamic/RTSE slippage). 6017 ExactOutAmountNotMatched and tick-array or bitmap errors are slippage-like.

JupiterZ quotes are firm quotes from 20+ market makers (Jupiter: zero slippage by design on eligible pairs), but market makers keep last-look rights, so a JupiterZ transaction cannot be modified after it is returned (use /build for CPI or custom instructions) and can still fail: /execute returns -2003 (quote expired) or -2004 (swap rejected). RFQ quotes carry a shorter-lived expireAt, while aggregator routes expire at lastValidBlockHeight, and Jupiter advises signing and submitting immediately because prices can still move inside the validity window.

Slippage and expiry failures seen in Jupiter's docs: program error 6001 SlippageToleranceExceeded (try higher fixed slippage or dynamic slippage), 6017 ExactOutAmountNotMatched (similar to slippage), DEX tick-array or bitmap-extension errors (the price moved out of range), and 6014 IncorrectTokenProgramID (likely a platform fee on a Token2022 token, also 0x177e). /order returns transaction as an empty string with an errorCode when it can quote but not build (for example insufficient funds or insufficient SOL for gas), and /execute returns -1005 when the blockhash expired before landing.
