Jupiter's user docs list further commissions: Limit Orders V1 and DCA V1 charge 0.1% flat, while Limit Orders V2 and DCA V2 charge 0.03% to 0.1% plus the Ultra routing fee of 0% to 0.5%. Swaps placed in the Jupiter Mobile app follow a separate fee schedule.

The older Metis Swap API could not take platform fees on Token-2022 mints: program error 6014 IncorrectTokenProgramID means the call tried to take a platform fee on a Token-2022 token. The Swap V2 referral program states support for SPL and Token-2022 mints.

Jupiter says Metis now ranks routes on estimated executed price, not quoted price. RTSE learns each market's gap between quoted and executed price from recent fills at different trade sizes (exponential moving averages plus failure-rate monitoring), and Predictive Execution simulates each candidate route onchain before choosing. Jupiter's April 2026 router post and trade press describe slippage-aware routing and just-in-time route finalization. None of these sources publishes before-and-after execution data.

JupiterZ is an RFQ path where market makers hold last-look execution rights, and its transactions cannot be modified after Jupiter returns them. RFQ quotes expire sooner than aggregator quotes, and /execute reports RFQ failures as -2003 (quote expired) and -2004 (swap rejected). Jupiter reports about $100M of daily JupiterZ volume with zero slippage.

When realized output falls below the slippage tolerance, Jupiter's swap program returns error 6001 SlippageToleranceExceeded. The docs advise a higher fixed slippage or dynamic slippage. Error 6017 ExactOutAmountNotMatched is 'similar to slippage', and tick-array or bitmap-extension errors from CLMM DEXes mean the price moved out of range. On /execute, code -1005 means the transaction expired before landing, usually because it was signed too late.

Slippage tolerance is a floor on output chosen at order time, not a forecast of cost. On /order, RTSE sets it from token category, recent slippage data and live failure rates and embeds it in the transaction, and a fixed slippageBps overrides RTSE. Jupiter's user docs warn that a high tolerance in manual mode can give unfavorable execution prices and a low one can make transactions fail.

Both the preprint and Jump's study measure fills against an external CEX reference price at fill time, not against the aggregator's quote. The preprint uses Bybit's size-weighted microprice converted through the USDC/USDT mid; Jump uses the best mid price across CEXs such as Binance. A quote-based comparison cannot see quote drift, but a reference-price comparison can.

Reclaim sweep recipe: list the wallet's token accounts under both the Token and Token-2022 programs, skip native (wrapped SOL) accounts, compute excess = lamports minus getMinimumBalanceForRentExemption(space) (cache one lookup per distinct size), then send WithdrawExcessLamports in batches of 20 per transaction, each instruction addressed to the program that owns its source. Simulate first. Raydium measured 270 compute units per instruction on Token and 1,414 on Token-2022. The 20-per-transaction figure comes from the 1,232-byte transaction limit.

A Jito bundle is a list of up to 5 fully signed transactions. They execute in the listed order, all-or-nothing, inside one slot. If any transaction fails, none of them commit, and a bundle cannot cross a slot boundary.

The public Block Engine limit is 1 request per second per IP per region. Exceeding it returns a 429 or a rate-limit error, and Jito raises limits on request through a ticket. Default sends no longer need an approved auth key. SDK code that still passes an auth keypair fails with '7 PERMISSION_DENIED: The supplied pubkey is not authorized to generate a token'. Pass no keypair.

Block Engine endpoints: https://mainnet.block-engine.jito.wtf (any region) plus amsterdam, dublin, frankfurt, london, ny, slc, singapore and tokyo subdomains of mainnet.block-engine.jito.wtf. Bundles use /api/v1/bundles and single transactions use /api/v1/transactions. A UUID is optional, passed as the x-jito-auth header or a uuid query parameter. Send bundles in base64, because base58 is deprecated and slow. The default limit is 1 request per second per IP per region.

Exposure differs sharply by app. The arXiv study's excess ratio (victim share divided by swap share, median over quarters) is 18.9 for Axiom, 11.1 Photon, 10.7 BullX, 10.6 GMGN, 8.8 Padre, 5.6 Trojan, 5.4 BonkBot and 0.7 for Jupiter Ultra; unattributed flow is 0.5. On single-victim sandwiches only, Axiom falls to 8.1 and Jupiter Ultra rises to 2.0. Ghost's wide-sandwich data agrees on direction: Axiom users were over 70% of extracted SOL, Bloom 10-15% and Photon 5-10%, while aggregators and wallets such as Jupiter and Phantom saw minimal impact. Jupiter Beta market rates: maker 0.005% (limit orders that rest), taker 0.035% (market and immediately-filled limit orders), liquidation fee 0.75% on crypto markets and 1% on stock markets. The page says the trading engine can adjust these.

Jupiter's borrow rate is tuned by outside risk managers and governance, not fixed. Gauntlet recommended cutting SOL/ETH/BTC from 0.008% to 0.007% per hour and USDC/USDT from 0.01% to 0.009% per hour on 2024-10-11, capping each change at 20%. In Feb 2025 Gauntlet and Chaos Labs proposed different curve changes.

Jupiter's Beta-market page lists a 0.005% (0.5 bps) maker fee on limit orders that rest on the book, a 0.035% (3.5 bps) taker fee on market orders and on limit orders that execute immediately, and a liquidation fee of 0.75% of position value on JUP, HYPE and ZEC and 1% on the stock markets. The page says the trading engine can adjust these rates.

Jupiter's Beta markets, GUM and Phoenix publish the same order-fee schedule: maker 0.5 bps (0.005%) and taker 3.5 bps (0.035%) of order value. Jupiter says its Beta markets run on GUM's orderbook engine. GUM states its maker fee 'is a charge, not a rebate'. Phoenix charges on matched notional, so a limit order is taker on the part that crosses and maker on any resting remainder. Referral discounts and builder fees (Phoenix Flight) change the all-in rate.

A resting order is not automatically a maker. On Velocity an order is a maker only with the post-only flag; without it a resting order can still match as a taker, pay the taker fee and earn no rebate. Jupiter's Beta trade form labels the fee as an estimate: the fee actually charged follows how the order filled. On Phoenix a limit order is taker on the crossed portion and maker on any remainder that rests.

Blacklist inputs have their own failure modes. JIP-15's validator list was publicly editable and an anonymous person added at least one wrong address, so Jito made edit rights private (5 March 2025). JIP-15 names a centralization risk because one detection method must stay private. A listed operator appealed that it had connected to a mempool provider that claimed to do only arbitrage. For JIP-22, Chainflow warned against relying on one data provider, Ghost; the JIP author agreed to triangulate sources, and the first wave used the Ghost API plus the Ghost, Pine and Solana Compass dashboards.

Revival attack: if a program zeroes an account's lamports but a later instruction in the same transaction refunds rent-exempt lamports, the account survives the runtime's end-of-transaction cleanup. Solana's program-security course documents this risk, and RareSkills notes that reassigning ownership to the System Program defuses it.

Refunding lamports to a caller-supplied account can fail or brick a program. The credit fails if the receiver would end below its rent-exempt minimum, because rent-paying states are rejected. It fails if the receiver is executable (as of OtterSec's May 2025 reading; SIMD-0162 proposes removing the flag). A writable account on the runtime's reserved list is silently demoted to read-only. OtterSec's fix: refund into a program-owned PDA vault and let users withdraw, and credit only non-executable accounts that stay rent-exempt after the credit.

Error strings and causes. 'Instruction does not support native tokens' (NativeNotSupported): WithdrawExcessLamports on a wrapped SOL account. 'Account does not support specified authority type' (AuthorityTypeNotSupported): a mint with no mint authority, unless the mint account itself signs. NotRentExempt: the source holds fewer lamports than the current minimum. A rerun after a sweep prints 'Reclaimable: 0 lamports from 0 accounts' until the next step. An oversized stake withdrawal fails with 'insufficient funds for instruction'. CloseAccount fails with NonNativeHasBalance on a funded non-nati

Token-2022 adds close blockers that the legacy program lacks. A token account with withheld transfer fees cannot close until the fees are harvested to the mint. Confidential-transfer and confidential-transfer-fee state must report closable. With CPI Guard lock_cpi set, a close made by CPI must send the lamports to the account owner (CpiGuardCloseAccountBlocked otherwise). A mint closes only if it has the MintCloseAuthority extension, the close authority signs and the supply is zero (MintHasSupply otherwise). A non-transferable token account lets its owner burn and close.

Revival attack: the runtime deletes a zero-lamport account only after the transaction completes. An attacker can invoke a close and add a transfer in the same transaction that refunds the rent-exempt lamports, so the account survives and the program may act on stale data. The Solana course advises zeroing the data and tagging a closed discriminator; RareSkills describes the same risk and the same attack path.

Marinade's SAM policy (page dated 4 Nov 2026) lists validators automatically each epoch, including any that sandwich in over 30% of the blocks they produce, with no prior warning. Listed validators get no Marinade stake and are redelegated first. The auction charges a one-time bond penalty in the first epoch listed of clearing_price + min(3 x effective_participating_bid, clearing_price) per 1,000 SOL of stake per epoch. Removal after a rightful listing needs at least one month of clean behaviour; repeat offenders are permanent.

Bitquery estimated $29.7 million of gross sandwich extraction on Solana between 30 October 2025 and 7 October 2026: 6,850,144 attacks by 2,545 bot wallets against 2,154,994 distinct wallets. The figure is gross. It values SOL at the minute of each attack and does not net out costs. In a separate 63-attack sample, bots kept 68% of gross proceeds and 18 attacks lost money after costs. Pump.fun's launch curve and PumpSwap held 96% of detected attacks. Bitquery says chain records cannot prove a bot saw an order beforehand, and some matching wallets may be fast traders.

Check how a sandwich count was built before quoting it. The arXiv study counts every transaction between the attacker's two legs as a victim even if only one was targeted, and it recomputes Solana app exposure on single-victim sandwiches only, which roughly halves Axiom's ratio (18.9 to 8.1). Ghost's 'momentum' and 'launch bot' wide sandwiches need not see the victim at all. Bitquery says chain records cannot prove a bot saw an order, and its $29.7M is gross. An Ethereum-rollup study (arXiv 2601.19570) found that over 95% of triples flagged by naive heuristics failed economic-consistency check

Pacifica borrows implicitly: a cross-margin account with spot collateral borrows USDC automatically when its equity excluding spot falls below zero. Default borrow APR is 1% at zero utilization, rises linearly to 10.95% at 80% utilization, then exponentially to 50% at 100%. Interest compounds per second, accrues every 60 seconds and is charged to the borrower's USDC balance hourly. Above 90% utilization, borrowing accounts cannot place new non-reduce-only perp orders; at 95% or more, pool-level deleveraging starts.

On Velocity, a resting limit order without the post-only flag can still match as a taker, pay the taker fee and earn no rebate. Velocity's docs call this the most common way a market-making strategy quietly loses its rebate.

Funding you owe may not have settled yet. Phoenix says pending, unsettled funding already affects account health and liquidation risk in real time. On Velocity funding is lazy: the rate updates when someone trades or a crank runs, and an update later than 20 minutes past the hour pushes the next one into the following period. Amounts owed between updates show as unrealized P&L and settle at the next trade, deposit, withdrawal or explicit settle in that market; a quiet market may not advance at all.

Rent is a deposit only because collection is off: the runtime rejects transitions that leave an account rent-paying, and every account must stay at or above the rent-exempt minimum to remain alive. Executable accounts cannot send or receive lamports, which constrains refund destinations.

CloseAccount deletes a token account and sends all its lamports, including the refundable rent, to a destination the closer chooses. If a close authority is set it signs; otherwise the owner signs. A non-native account must hold zero tokens first (Token-2022 error NonNativeHasBalance). A frozen account with zero tokens can still close. A wrapped SOL account can close with a balance and returns the underlying SOL too. The source and destination must differ. The account that paid to create an associated token account (ATA) does not automatically receive the refund.

Rent is a deposit only because collection is off. SIMD-0084 (Activated) stopped collecting rent from accounts and paying it to validators, and creating a rent-paying account already fails. After each transaction an account must hold 0 lamports (closed) or at least its minimum; SIMD-0392 states the check as post_exec_balance == 0 or >= min_allowed_balance. Executable accounts cannot send or receive lamports.

SIMD-0437 lowers lamports_per_byte from 6,960 to 696 in five steps, each behind its own feature gate: 6,333, 5,080, 2,575, 1,322 and 696 (effective cuts of 9%, 27%, 63%, 81% and 90%). A sixth gate can reset the rate to 6,960. The SIMD allows the next step only after a risk analysis based on existing safeguards and empirical data, and says risk grows superlinearly as the cut deepens.

The classic Token and p-token instruction lists contain no mint-close instruction: CloseAccount covers token accounts, and AuthorityType has no mint-close variant (inferred from the absence in the instruction list). A classic mint's deposit therefore cannot be refunded by closing. The mint authority can still sweep the excess above the minimum with WithdrawExcessLamports. If the authority is revoked and the mint account cannot sign, nothing can sweep it; Raydium says LaunchLab's base mint is stranded this way by design.

A Zellic audit finding reports that a claimable-token close flow can be blocked by a dust attack: an attacker sends a tiny amount of the same mint to the account before the close, the balance is no longer zero, and the rent cannot be reclaimed. The page returned HTTP 403, so only the search-result summary was seen.

Fake 'reclaim your rent' sites are a live phishing pattern. A MalwareTips scan flags solclaimer.app as a wallet-draining page posing as a rent reclaimer, and PhishDestroy flags refundsolana.net as a Solana-impersonating drainer. A legitimate close should only send rent to the owner's own wallet; any transaction that adds SetAuthority or Assign, or names another destination, is the warning sign.

Stake accounts: the BPF stake program computes the reserve from the live Rent sysvar (process_withdraw uses rent.minimum_balance(data_len)), so excess on a pre-reduction stake account can be withdrawn with the withdraw authority (solana withdraw-stake), up to balance minus delegated stake minus the current reserve. The parsed meta.rentExemptReserve field still reads 2,282,880 because SIMD-0490 (Activated) holds that deprecated field fixed for new accounts and calls the move to the Rent sysvar a hard blocker on rent reduction. Compute the reserve with getMinimumBalanceForRentExemption(200).

SIMD-0437 merged on 2026-01-20 after review that replaced explicit numeric advancement criteria with the rule 'proceed only if a risk analysis indicates it is safe'. On 2026-02-12 a reviewer noted that lowering rent requires changing how Rent is used in the stake program (and possibly the token programs). SIMD-0490 (stake v5.0.0, Activated) then made the Rent sysvar authoritative. No organised objection to the cut appears in the SIMD record; the debate was about advancement criteria and safeguards, and the Foundation and Anza authors both advocate the cut.

In the v1 transaction format the priority fee is an absolute lamport total in the message config (no per-CU price, no multiplication, no rounding), ComputeBudget instructions are ignored, and an unset CU limit defaults to zero rather than 200,000 per instruction. The v1 fee is 5,000 x numRequiredSignatures plus priorityFee.

A like-for-like venue comparison adds up entry and exit fees (or base fee), price impact or slippage, signed funding or the one-sided borrow fee, the liquidation fee, and referral or builder adjustments. Chaos Labs lists opening fees, slippage and liquidation costs as the part that funding-versus-borrow tables omit. MadeOnSol lists entry and exit fees, spread, slippage, spot borrow interest, liquidation fees and collateral transfer cost. Jupiter's trade form shows a live Total Fees breakdown (open fee, price impact, borrow fees due, transaction fee, rent) before confirmation.

Defensive bundling is a real cost. IMC counted 864,889,302 single-transaction Jito bundles (86% of that class) with tips of 100,000 lamports or less, which it reads as bundles sent to avoid sandwiches rather than to gain priority. Users spent about $2.42M on those tips, about $0.00286 per bundle. A transaction inside its own Jito bundle cannot be placed inside an attacker's bundle, because bundles cannot be nested. Jupiter's 'MEV protection' option sends a length-one Jito bundle. Helius says Jito-only MEV Protect modes carry slightly higher fees and many Telegram bot users do not turn them on.

Under SIMD-0553 the CU limit would become a direct cost even at zero priority fee, because the resource fee uses requested cost units. Foundation modelling finds that even with perfect requests only about 28% of transactions would see a fee increase under 10%. A vote transaction with 3,765 requested cost units would pay 2,500 + 1,883 lamports instead of 5,000 (-12.3%). Aggregator swaps would pay the most. Tight limits from simulation would matter more than they do now.

Validators execute the pre-sequenced result, can fall back to their own TPU, and can run plugins for application-controlled ordering rules. Both Jupiter risk advisers frame cost as more than the headline rate. Gauntlet writes tradingFee = (baseFee + orderBookImpact) x tradeSize. SIMD-0170 (Activated, Anza) reserves only 3,000 CUs (MAX_BUILTIN_ALLOCATION_COMPUTE_UNIT_LIMIT) per builtin instruction when no limit is requested, instead of 200,000, so builtin-only transactions stop over-reserving block CUs. Builtin-only transactions that relied on the default can now fail and should set an explicit limit. Agave PR #3755 was closed unmerged on 2024-11-27; PR #3799 merged on 2024-12-05 (commit 3e9af14f). Block packing reserves each transaction's requested cost first and releases the unused part only after execution reports the CUs consumed (SIMD-0170 motivation; Solana Foundation, 2026-08-21). Over-requested limits therefore take block room from other transactions while the transaction runs. Priority is fee per requested cost, so for a fixed total fee a larger limit also lowers the transaction's priority. In Anza's hypothetical token-transfer example, requesting a 10 MB loaded-data limit instead of the 64 MB default raises the priority score from 0.30 to 0.63.

Helius's research post (2024-06-01) says its RPC data show that transactions with priority fees 'are more likely to land, and when they do, they land quicker across the board', and that higher fees give 'a greater likelihood for inclusion'. The statement rests on a chart whose values are not in the page text. It compares transactions with a fee against transactions without one, not fee percentiles. That differs from Chorus One, which compares fee tiers among transactions that already landed.

Gasless swaps cost extra. The extra is a fixed amount rather than a percentage, so small trades pay proportionally more; Jupiter says gasless is offered only when the recovered gas is within 10% of the trade (about a $10 minimum). In Swap V2 the extra shows in top-level feeBps but not in platformFee.feeBps (documented example: 5 bps platform plus 7 bps gasless gives feeBps 12). JupiterZ RFQ routes are gasless

Jito warns that skipped slots produce uncled blocks, and transactions from a bundle can be rebroadcast from them. Such rebroadcast transactions do not respect bundle atomicity or revert protection, so they can land and revert on-chain. Jito advises putting the tip inside the main transaction rather than a standalone tip transaction, and adding pre/post account checks.

A Feb 2025 community proposal to move Jupiter's borrow fee to a utilization-banded step schedule (every 8 hours, floor 0.0001%/hr, ceiling 0.05%/hr) got no vote and no formal decision. The author replaced it with a broader fee proposal. It is evidence of how traders see always-on borrow fees versus funding that can be zero or negative, not of current policy.

Same-day cost snapshot (Gauntlet, 2025-01-30): Jupiter SOL-PERP borrow 33.1152% APR versus Flash Trade 39.3613%. Annualized SOL-PERP funding that day was +7.81% Drift, -0.83% Binance, +10.95% Hyperliquid, +2.40% dYdX and +58.98% Zeta; BTC-PERP ranged from -53.87% (Zeta) to +52.44% (dYdX). A forum author put Jupiter's SOL borrow at about 0.003% per hour (~30% APR) on 2025-02-20. Funding is a signed number that differs by venue and asset; Jupiter's JLP-market borrow fee is always a cost.

Where to read live values instead of trusting a doc table: Jupiter's trade form (Total Fees breakdown; market-header borrow rate) and the on-chain custody account (jumpRateState; FundingRateState.cumulativeInterestRate against each position's cumulativeInterestSnapshot); Velocity's per-market fee, dead-zone and ramp values on the live market accounts (its fee table loads 'live from the program'); Phoenix's REST endpoints GET /v1/funding/{symbol}/rates, GET /v1/funding/overview and GET /v1/trader/{authority}/funding-history.

Helius 'MEV Protect' is an opt-in routing feature (off by default; add mev-protect=true to the endpoint URL). It steers transactions away from validators statistically linked to sandwiching, which excludes roughly 3-4 million SOL of stake at any time. It works with sendTransaction and sendBundle, still needs normal tip and priority fee, can slightly cut inclusion rate, and reduces rather than removes risk.

A platform that sponsors rent can lose it when users close accounts: the refund goes to the destination the closing signer names, not back to the sponsor. Turnkey writes that refunded lamports 'may go to the signer, not back to you'. Its mitigations: reuse a constrained set of token accounts instead of create-and-close loops; strip SPL Token CloseAccount instructions (discriminator 9) before submission; set Jupiter wrapAndUnwrapSol to false and manage wSOL explicitly; apply spend caps, rate limits and alerts. Filtering is weaker if users can export or control the signer key.

Solana has no global public mempool: clients forward transactions straight to upcoming leaders, and unprocessed transactions expire after about 150 blocks (~1 minute). The Solana docs say this shrinks the MEV surface compared with public-mempool chains. It does not remove it, because a sandwich only needs someone with early sight of the victim's order (a leader, an RPC or relay, or an app).

On Velocity the taker pays a tiered fee on filled notional and the maker earns a rebate paid out of that fee. The fee is denominated in USDT and applied to the position's cost basis rather than billed separately. A round trip pays the taker fee twice.

JLP Loans couple to short-side borrow cost. USDC lent through JLP Loans counts in the USDC custody's utilization, which sets the borrow fee for shorts. Chaos Labs' 2025-08-14 update sized USDC borrowing so it would not disrupt short positions (USDC utilization by shorts peaked near 20% over 12 months, so a borrow limit of 80% and a target utilization of 90%; maintenance margin 83%, liquidation margin 86%). JLP Loans interest compounds and is added to debt, unlike the perp borrow fee.

A wrapped SOL account stores its rent reserve in is_native and sets amount = lamports - reserve when it is initialized. SyncNative recomputes both from the current Rent. After a rate cut, SyncNative therefore turns the excess into wrapped token balance instead of returning SOL, which is why WithdrawExcessLamports rejects native accounts. The exits are CloseAccount (works with a balance and returns rent plus the underlying SOL) and UnwrapLamports (discriminant 45; partial unwrap; non-native accounts get NonNativeNotSupported). Stake incentives fed validator-side sandwiching. Helius (Jan 2025) noted Marinade's pay-for-stake auction let sandwiching validators outbid others (winning APY 13.73% and top-ten bids up to 18.27%, versus about 9.4% for validators charging 0% commission and 0% MEV commission). It also noted the DeezNode-linked validator grew from 307.9k to 802.5k SOL of stake between epochs 697 and 709, 19.89% of it from Marinade. Ghost's May 2025 talk and a May 2025 Marinade forum proposal reported the same pattern; the proposal asserted most high-bidding validators were sandwich attackers.

The Foundation prices rent in USD at a SOL price of $77.94: a 165-byte token account deposit is $0.159 now and $0.0159 after step 5, and one million token accounts cost $159,000 now versus $15,900. Dollar values scale linearly with the SOL price. Solana Compass showed SOL near $90 on 2026-11-06, which would put the deposit near $0.134 at step 2 and near $0.018 at step 5 (derived here, not reported).

Transaction v1 (SIMD-0385) is live on mainnet and changes the unit of the priority fee. QuickNode (guide updated 2026-10-21) says feature gate txv1aq4pp281K9um3tnPgkfX8UqtFT6wcVW3hNezGLL went active on testnet at epoch 1025 (2026-09-01) and on mainnet at slot 447,120,000 (2026-09-15). The SIMD lists status Activated. A v1 message carries its priority fee in a header config field as a total in lamports (an 8-byte u64, mask bits 0 and 1). Legacy and v0 transactions use a SetComputeUnitPrice instruction priced in micro-lamports per compute unit. If the priority-fee bits are unset, the fee is 0. C

getFeeForMessage, the fee in simulateTransaction and meta.fee in getTransaction each return one lamport total (base fee plus priority fee), not a base-fee-only number; getRecentPrioritizationFees reports priority fees only. Block metadata exposes computeUnitsConsumed and costUnits, so a client can compare consumed CUs with the scheduler cost. SIMD-0553 would keep these scalar totals but add the resource fee to them.

Fee scale in mid-2026: Solana Compass analytics put daily validator fee revenue near 7,900 SOL in early August 2026 (about 820 SOL base fees, 5,600 SOL priority fees, 1,500 SOL Jito tips). SIMD-0553 cites about 648 SOL per day burned from signature fees at roughly 3,000 TPS, against about 60,000 SOL per day of inflation (May 2026 data). Priority fees therefore dwarf base fees in SOL terms. The two figures measure different things and months.

The standard RPC estimate was criticised as insufficient in Agave issue 3332 (opened 2024-10-28). It reported a 0 fee for a program whose transactions did not land even at 10k micro-lamports per compute unit. The issue asks for an RPC that takes a target inclusion probability, and as of 2026-11-06 it is still OPEN. Helius also says the core RPC estimate ignores Jito's influence, and warns that each provider's custom API is a soft form of vendor lock-in.

Default CU price is 0 micro-lamports, so a transaction with no SetComputeUnitPrice instruction pays no priority fee. SetComputeUnitPrice takes a u64 in micro-lamports (discriminator 3); SetComputeUnitLimit takes a u32 (discriminator 2) and any value above 1,400,000 is clamped to 1,400,000.

BAM (Block Assembly Marketplace) launched on Solana mainnet in September 2025. BAM nodes run an encrypted mempool inside trusted execution environments (AMD SEV-SNP). They order transactions in periodic auctions, ranking by priority fee per compute unit (Jito tips count for bundles) and handling conflicting transactions first-in first-out. BAM validators execute that order. Jito has run every BAM node so far.

A higher compute unit price did not guarantee landing in spring 2024. On 2024-03-22 Phantom's developer-relations manager said that adding a higher fee did not improve success rates during memecoin congestion. The Block (2024-04-08) reported that many apps sent no priority fee at all and blamed bot spam; the fixes it named were client bug fixes, QUIC changes and a 1.18 scheduling update. Later scheduler changes belong to the landing-probability sibling concept.

Each ComputeBudget instruction executes as a builtin no-op that consumes 150 CUs (DEFAULT_COMPUTE_UNITS = 150 in Agave's compute-budget program), so SetComputeUnitLimit plus SetComputeUnitPrice spend 300 CUs of the budget they set. Include them in the transaction you simulate so unitsConsumed already counts them.

Triton's percentile extension to getRecentPrioritizationFees takes an integer from 1 to 10000 (5000 = median, 9000 = 90th percentile). Per block it takes the percentile of non-vote compute-unit prices. With account addresses it takes the percentile over transactions write-locking each account and returns the highest of those values. Self-hosted nodes need Triton's getrpf patch (Agave issue 3332, PR 217).

Helius counts non-vote transactions that set no compute unit price as zero-fee samples. This is why Min and Low often return 0 and why Helius numbers sit below percentiles computed over priced transactions only.

No surveyed estimator outputs a landing probability. Each reports a price distribution drawn from transactions that already reached a block. Agave's cache stores fees of landed transactions. Triton takes percentiles of the compute-unit prices paid by non-vote transactions in each block. Helius's open-source estimator samples only successful non-vote transactions and skips any transaction with meta.err set. A percentile therefore describes what landed transactions paid. It does not give the chance that a given bid lands, and bids that never reached a block are invisible to it. That last step is

In the open-source Atlas code, the 'recommended' option returns max(Medium estimate, 10,000 micro-lamports per compute unit), rounded up (const MIN_RECOMMENDED_PRIORITY_FEE = 10_000.0). The Helius documentation pages read for this run never state that floor or explain what 'recommended' does, and QuickNode's docs give no formula for their own 'recommended' value. Each vendor's 'recommended' is therefore an opaque composite, and the Helius one can sit well above the network median.

The stock getRecentPrioritizationFees RPC answers 'what did the cheapest landed bid pay', not 'what will land'. In Agave master (read 2026-11-06), PrioritizationFeeCache keeps the last 150 blocks (MAX_NUM_RECENT_BLOCKS = 150). For each slot, get_prioritization_fees returns the block's minimum compute-unit price. If you pass writable accounts, it raises that value to the highest per-account minimum (std::cmp::max). Triton calls the stock value a minimum that is 'often zero'. Chainstack calls each value 'the floor for that slot'.

Agave issue 3332 (opened 2024-10-28, label 'community') asks for a standard RPC that returns a fee for a target inclusion chance. It says the stock RPC returned prioritizationFee 0 for the loader program, yet most of that program's transactions did not land even at 10k micro-lamports per compute unit. A 2024-12-04 comment sketches two signatures: ({computeUnits, writeLockedAccounts, pLanding}) => microLamports, and (transactionMessageBytes, pLanding) => microLamports, the second using PID-style prediction. Leaders rank transactions by reward per unit of cost: Priority = reward x 1,000,000 / (cost + 1), where reward is the priority fee plus the non-burned half of the base fee and cost is the scheduler cost above. Anza states Block Packing Priority = Reward / Transaction Cost and shows a token transfer needing about 6k execution CUs whose total cost is near 22k CUs under the default 64 MiB loaded-data assumption, which lowers its priority for the same fee.

Jupiter's fee page lists the Solana transaction cost as a SOL network fee plus a priority fee that Jupiter sets automatically; the trade form has no priority-fee or Jito-tip setting. Sibling concepts cover those costs.

Manual-mode swaps on jup.ag carry no Jupiter commission. The user still pays Solana network fees, which are owed whether or not the trade succeeds, plus any Jito tip the user chooses. A March 2025 forum thread asking Jupiter to end 'free' manual mode also treats manual swaps as commission-free.

The Block Engine's sendTransaction forwards one transaction to the validator with MEV protection by default and always sets skip_preflight=true. Adding ?bundleOnly=true sends it as a single-transaction bundle for revert protection. On success the bundle ID is in the x-bundle-id response header. For sendTransaction, Jito suggests a 70/30 split of spend between priority fee and Jito tip. For sendBundle only the Jito tip matters.

Jito's docs state a minimum bundle tip of 1000 lamports and warn it may be too low during high demand. Alchemy repeats the 1,000-lamport floor and says contested MEV opportunities need substantially higher tips. Helius's older MEV report gives 10,000 lamports instead (see disagreements).

Live check on 2026-11-06: getFeeForMessage priced a one-signer message at 5,000 lamports and a two-signer message at 10,000.

Estimating the cost of a bidding strategy from successful transactions alone understates it. Bitquery says failed transactions pay a higher average fee than successful ones and that a substantial share of all fees paid on Solana goes to failed transactions (no data window stated). The ISSTA 2025 study finds the same pattern: failed transactions incurred higher fees than successful ones at every quantile, yet sat deeper in blocks (median position 592 against 529), which the authors read as being outcompeted.

A higher priority fee raises ordering priority but does not guarantee inclusion. Helius says the scheduler gives no guarantee, Chorus One found no fee threshold above which transactions consistently landed faster, and OrbitFlare says the fee only orders transactions while the submission path gets them to the leader.

Application choice changes sandwich exposure. In the arXiv study's 'excess ratio' (lower is better), Jupiter Ultra scores 0.7 overall, against Axiom 18.9, Photon 11.1, and BullX and GMGN above 10. Jupiter's Beta markets (JUP, HYPE, ZEC, and the stock perps SPCX, SNDK, SKHYNIX) run on the GUM orderbook engine, not the JLP pool. They replace the base, price impact and borrow fees with a taker or maker fee per order plus an hourly funding rate that longs and shorts pay each other. jitodontfront: add any valid public key starting with 'jitodontfront' (it need not exist on-chain; mark it read-only and non-signer) to an instruction. The Jito block engine then rejects any bundle containing that transaction unless it sits at index 0. Several flagged transactions may lead a bundle if they are contiguous and share a signer. It works with Jito sendTransaction and sendBundle and supports address lookup tables.

jitodontfront covers only the Jito block engine: transactions sent straight to validators, or ordered by other software, are not protected. Jito's own disclaimer says it 'may help reduce sandwich attacks but is not guaranteed to do so' and does not address ordering by third parties. Heimbach et al. read the guarantee as no front-running inside a Jito bundle and nothing beyond that path.

Validators run Jito-Solana, a modified Agave client. Searchers, apps and bots send bundles and transactions to the Jito Block Engine over gRPC or JSON-RPC. The Block Engine forwards winning bundles to the current leader. Tips go to validators and their stakers after Jito's fee. Jito's GitBook adds that bundles are not forwarded between validators.

Architecture: Jito-Solana is Jito's fork of the Solana (Agave) validator. A validator running it connects to a Jito Block Engine. Searchers, dApps and bots submit transactions and bundles to the Block Engine over gRPC or JSON-RPC. The Block Engine simulates bundles, picks the most profitable combination and sends it to the leader, which executes the bundles atomically and collects the tips. The tips are then redistributed to the validator and its stakers.

The stock getRecentPrioritizationFees RPC returns the minimum prioritization fee seen per recent slot, over a node cache of up to 150 blocks. That minimum is often 0, so it is a poor basis for a landing fee.

Helius getPriorityFeeEstimate exposes six levels: Min, Low (25th percentile), Medium (50th, recommended default), High (75th), VeryHigh (above the 95th, not outlier-trimmed, with extra headroom) and UnsafeMax (the maximum observed). The docs warn that VeryHigh and UnsafeMax are landing targets, not measures of what the network pays.

Estimate scope decides usefulness. With neither a serialized transaction nor writable accountKeys, Helius returns a global estimate, which it says is not a fee to pay. Passing the writable accounts scopes the estimate to the local market you compete in. Practitioner guides likewise say to base the fee on the accounts the transaction touches, not on network-wide medians.

Landing-rate comparisons are easily distorted. RPC Fast says to hold the fee, transaction shape and commitment level constant across paths, count at one commitment level, and divide confirmed sends by all attempts including failures. It also says a path tested at a higher fee can look faster without being so.

Optional /order parameters trade away defaults. A receiver or payer parameter removes Dflow and OKX from the race, and excludeRouters removes the router it names. Referral parameters keep all four routers but stop automatic gas sponsorship. A fixed slippageBps replaces RTSE without restricting routing. Any such parameter flips the response mode from 'ultra' to 'manual', which Jupiter says can change price or swap success.

A quote goes stale fast. Aggregator routes (Metis, Dflow, OKX) stay valid until lastValidBlockHeight and RFQ routes until expireAt, but prices can still move against the user inside that window. Jupiter's guidance is to sign and submit as soon as the order arrives.

The Jupiter hourly borrow rate comes from a per-asset jump-rate (dual-slope) utilization curve: annual rate rises slowly from a minimum to a target utilization, then steeply to a maximum, divided by 8,760 hours. Longs use the market asset's utilization; shorts use the USDC custody's. On-chain, each position stores a cumulativeInterestSnapshot and the custody keeps FundingRateState (cumulativeInterestRate, hourlyFundingDbps).

Jupiter's fee page defines borrow fee (USD) = position size x hourly borrow rate x hours open. The hourly rate comes from a per-asset utilization jump-rate curve (annual rate divided by 8,760) that rises slowly to a target utilization and steeply above it. The fee accrues on the full position size without compounding and is taken from collateral whenever the position or its collateral changes. Longs use the market asset's curve and utilization; shorts use the USDC custody's.

Hyperliquid's funding is peer-to-peer with no fee collected on payments, and it pays position size x oracle price x funding rate (the oracle price, not the mark price). Jupiter's Beta markets compute each hourly payment on the position value at the time it is applied.

Live parameters are readable, so read them before costing a trade. Jupiter's custody accounts (SOL 7xS2gz2bTp3fwCC7knJvUWTEU9Tycczu6VhJYKgi1wdz, BTC 5Pv3gM9JrFFH883SWAhvJC9RPYmo8UNxuFtv5bMMALkm, ETH AQCGyheWPLeo6Qp9WpYS9m3Qj479t7R636N9ey1rEjEn) hold tradeImpactFeeScalar and jumpRateState. Pacifica publishes borrow pool state at GET /api/v1/loan_pool. Velocity's docs tell readers to read the live market account for admin-set funding and fee values.

GUM and Jupiter's Beta markets pay funding every hour, on the hour (UTC), on the position held at that moment. A positive rate means longs pay shorts; a negative rate means shorts pay longs. GUM adds that a position opened and closed between two hourly marks pays no funding, that GUM takes no fee on funding, and that paying funding lowers account value and so moves the position closer to liquidation. Hyperliquid likewise says funding is purely peer-to-peer with no fee collected on the payments.

Jupiter's JLP markets and the funding venues have opposite holding-cost shapes. On JLP markets (SOL, ETH, wBTC) every trader pays the pool a borrow fee whichever side they hold, so no one receives holding income; Chaos Labs says short hedges are 'not currently viable' there for lack of a funding rate. On funding venues the payer is whichever side holds the perp away from the oracle, so funding can be a cost, zero or a credit. MadeOnSol warns not to assume a short on a pool venue earns what shorts earn on Drift. Jupiter's Beta markets switched this shape to funding.

Jupiter's own pages disagree about the borrow-fee input. The fees page says the rate comes from the custody's jumpRateState utilization curve and that no separate utilization factor applies. The developer custody-account page still calls hourlyFundingDbps 'a constant used to calculate the hourly borrow fees'. Gauntlet's May 2024 post defined the older model as hourly rate = utilization x max hourly rate. A formula that multiplies by utilization again, or uses one constant hourly rate, likely follows the older model; read the live custody account and the trade form instead.

Slippage tolerance caps what a sandwich can take but does not prevent it. The Solana docs call limiting slippage the single most effective defense. Gerzon et al. cite prior work showing slippage acts as a cap, not a block. Helius and Ghost note that memecoin traders accept high slippage to land fast, which is what attackers exploit.

Batch reclaim cost is small. Raydium's reclaim tool packs about 20 instructions per transaction (116 accounts = 6 transactions at the 5,000-lamport base fee each); WithdrawExcessLamports uses about 270 CU for SPL Token and 1,414 CU for Token-2022. Its SDK demo `reclaimRent.ts` defaults to DRY_RUN=true.

Velocity charges hourly funding of (1/24) x (market TWAP - oracle TWAP) / oracle TWAP after two corrections. A per-market dead zone (admin-set, in bps of the oracle TWAP) drops small gaps as noise. A floor of oracle TWAP / 3333 keeps funding non-zero. Funding updates lazily on trades or permissionless cranks, so a quiet market may accrue no funding until the next action there.

WithdrawExcessLamports also rescues SOL that someone sent directly to a Token-Program-owned account, which could not be moved before. The Solana docs call this SOL 'previously stranded', and the interface comment describes the instruction as a way to rescue SOL sent to any token-program-owned account while leaving only the rent-exempt lamports.

The rate cut moves no lamports. An account funded before a step keeps its balance. The gap between that balance and the new minimum is excess that only the account's authority can withdraw (for a program-owned account, only the owning program). Nothing is refunded automatically and no deadline applies; the excess stays in the account until withdrawn. AMBCrypto concludes the change resembles capital recovery, not an airdrop.

The 2026 arXiv study (Heimbach, Solmaz, Oez, Ferreira Torres; Category Labs, ETH Zurich, Flashbots, Univ. of Lisbon) identifies 28.0 million sandwich attacks on Solana against transactions meant to be protected from front-running. That is far above Tron (38,567), Ethereum (30,607) and Base (1,889). The press coverage of this paper repeats the 28M figure, so the two sources share one origin.

Two independently built detectors agree on recent volume of roughly 20,000 sandwiches a day. Heimbach et al. report daily volume settling near 20,000 after the Oct 2025 JitoSOL delisting. Bitquery counted 6,850,144 attacks by 2,545 bot wallets between 30 Oct 2025 and 7 Oct 2026 (about 20,000 a day, derived over 342 days).

Anza's lead economist Max Resnick said in mid-2025 that the 'sandwiching rate [is] way down', crediting improved transaction targeting (fewer validators see each transaction) over blacklists, whose targets can re-appear under new identities. The Blockworks piece (12 Jul 2025, read through a Bitget mirror) gives no figures.

Stake programs have removed sandwich-linked validators in waves. The Solana Foundation delegation program did so in Jun 2024. Marinade's stake auction blocklisted 73 validators under MIP-9 (posted 7 Feb 2025). On the JitoSOL pool, JIP-15 was executed in May 2025 with 50-epoch removals, and the first wave under JIP-22 and JIP-23 blacklisted 28 validators (update of 17 Sep 2025). Heimbach et al. add a further JitoSOL delisting in Oct 2025.

Blacklists alone have not stopped validator-side sandwiching. Marinade said sandwichers 'simply spun up new validators faster than we could identify and block them' (24 Jun 2025). Marinade forum posters noted attackers just change identity addresses. Ghost's talk said new validators can take stake and start sandwiching quickly. Heimbach et al. conclude each intervention removes or weakens one exposure source without eliminating the attacks.

Two independent measurements put late-2025 to 2026 attack volume near 20,000 per day. The arXiv study's final era (after October 2025) averages about 20,000 sandwiches per day. Bitquery counted 6,850,144 attacks between 30 October 2025 and 7 October 2026, which is about 20,000 per day by our arithmetic (342 days). The methods differ and Bitquery reports gaps in exchange and block coverage, so this shows the order of magnitude, not exact agreement.

The Solana Foundation acted before the stake pools. A 7 May policy post from its validator relations lead, Tim Garcia, said operators 'participating in a private mempool to sandwich attack transactions' would be rejected from the delegation program (SFDP). On 10 June 2024 the Foundation removed a group of operators for sandwiching; they lose delegated SOL but may keep validating. Garcia said enforcement was ongoing as the Foundation detected operators in mempools that allow sandwich attacks. The Block gives no operator count and no detection method.

Drift was exploited on 2026-04-01 for about $295M by a DPRK-affiliated actor (per Drift, confirmed by Mandiant). Trading and borrowing were suspended, and the protocol was rebuilt as the USDT-settled Velocity exchange. Drift's 2026-05-05 plan funds recovery tokens from quarterly exchange revenue, up to $127.5M from Tether and up to $20M from partners. Anyone quoting old Drift maker/taker or funding numbers is quoting a venue that no longer exists in that form.

Drift's spot borrow/lend markets shared a single liquidity pool, and interest accrual on spot balances stopped at the 2026-04-01 pause. Drift said users would not owe outstanding interest on relaunch. This is the only official statement found on Drift borrow interest; the borrow-rate formula itself was not retrieved.

Velocity lenders earn the borrow rate x utilization minus an insurance-fund factor and a protocol factor, both taken from the deposit-side gain. Borrowers pay the same rate whatever those factors are. Interest compounds through deposit and borrow indices, and no interest accrues at zero utilization.

Fee tiers key on rolling volume, and the windows differ. Pacifica uses 14-day volume, updated daily, with subaccounts pooled into the master account's tier. Velocity uses trailing 30-day taker plus maker volume; each counter decays linearly to zero over 30 days, a fill's volume promotes the very next fill, and liquidation volume counts for both sides.

A rent sponsor that pre-funds accounts can lose the deposit. Turnkey's rent sponsorship (an Enterprise-plan feature, off by default) pre-funds the signer for new accounts, and the refund goes to the close destination, usually the signer or owner, not the sponsor. Turnkey's mitigations: strip CloseAccount (discriminator 9) before submission, set Jupiter's wrapAndUnwrapSol to false and manage wrapped SOL explicitly, reuse a constrained set of token accounts, and apply deny policies, spend caps and monitoring.

Rent-exempt minimums by account size (lamports): empty 0-byte 890,880 -> 650,240 after step 2 -> 89,088 after step 5; 82-byte mint 1,461,600 -> 1,066,800 -> 146,160; 165-byte token account 2,039,280 -> 1,488,440 -> 203,928; 200-byte stake account 2,282,880 -> 1,666,240 -> 228,288. The 0-byte pre-reduction figure (0.00089088 SOL) is independently shown by OtterSec's `solana rent 0` example.

The rent reduction moves no lamports. Existing accounts keep their old, higher balances; the gap between balance and the new minimum is 'excess' that the owner can withdraw. For a 165-byte token account the excess is 183,711 lamports after step 1 and 1,835,352 lamports at step 5; a 182-byte Token-2022 account holds 194,370 excess at step 1.

In the p-token processor, WithdrawExcessLamports returns TokenError::NativeNotSupported for wrapped SOL accounts and TokenError::NotRentExempt if the source holds fewer lamports than Rent::get()?.minimum_balance(data_len). It reads the minimum from the Rent sysvar at call time. Wrapped SOL rent can therefore be recovered only by closing the account.

Not every account type can return excess in place. Stake accounts use the stake withdraw authority (and SIMD-0490 pins rent_exempt_reserve at 2,282,880 lamports). Program PDAs need an instruction in the owning program. Raydium CLMM positions and OpenBook open-orders accounts return rent only through their own close instructions. System-owned wallets have nothing to reclaim.

Rent-exempt minimums in lamports at rates 6,960 / 5,080 / 696: 0-byte account 890,880 / 650,240 / 89,088; 82-byte mint 1,461,600 / 1,066,800 / 146,160; 165-byte token account 2,039,280 / 1,488,440 / 203,928; 200-byte stake account 2,282,880 / 1,666,240 / 228,288. A 165-byte token account needs 1,855,569 at step 1, 754,475 at step 3 and 387,346 at step 4. OtterSec's solana rent 0 output (0.00089088 SOL) independently confirms the old 0-byte figure.

WithdrawExcessLamports (discriminator 38, in the Token and Token-2022 programs) moves lamports above the current rent-exempt minimum out of a token account, mint or multisig. It takes no amount: the program reads Rent at call time and leaves exactly the minimum. It does not close the account or change token balances or mint supply. Running it again on an account already at the minimum moves 0 lamports. Signer: the owner for a token account; the mint authority for a mint, or the mint account itself if the mint has no authority; the M-of-N signers for a multisig.

Revival attack: a program that closes an account by zeroing its lamports does not delete it until the transaction ends. An attacker adds a transfer in the same transaction that refunds the rent, and the account survives. Safe closing moves the lamports, reassigns the owner to the System Program and shrinks the data. Current Anchor close() does this: it credits the destination, sets lamports to 0, calls assign(system_program::ID) and resize(0), and rejects closing an account into itself.

SPL Token CloseAccount deletes a token account and sends all its lamports (rent plus any extra) to a destination chosen by the owner or the close authority, who signs. It fails with InvalidAccountData if source and destination are the same account, and with NonNativeHasBalance if a non-native account still holds tokens. A frozen account with a zero balance can still close. The account that paid to create an associated token account gets nothing back automatically.

Stake accounts release their excess through a normal stake withdrawal. The stake program computes the reserve from the Rent sysvar and ignores Meta.rent_exempt_reserve, which it sets to 2,282,880 for compatibility (source comment: set to its historical value unconditionally, but ignored in the stake program). SIMD-0490 holds the field at 2,282,880 for new stake accounts and says to prefer the Rent sysvar. Chainstack's worked example withdraws 616,640 lamports from an undelegated 200-byte stake account at step 2.

Only the owning program can debit a program-owned account, so excess rent on a program's PDAs needs an instruction in that program. The Foundation's checklist: verify the account is owned by the program, verify the authority signer, read the floor from the Rent sysvar, move only the excess, and conserve lamports across the transaction. Programs you do not control often have no such instruction.

Token-2022 adds close checks beyond a zero balance. A token account with non-zero withheld transfer fees fails with AccountHasWithheldTransferFees. A confidential-transfer account needs zero pending and available encrypted balances (ConfidentialTransferAccountHasBalance). With CPI Guard locked, a close inside a CPI fails (CpiGuardCloseAccountBlocked) unless the destination is the owner. A Token-2022 mint closes only with the MintCloseAuthority extension and zero supply (MintHasSupply otherwise). Token-2022 WithdrawExcessLamports needs the owner (not the close authority) and fails inside a CPI

Client support: getWithdrawExcessLamportsInstruction is exported by @solana-program/token (the Token program), and the Token-2022 program exposes the same instruction through @solana-program/token-2022. Docs use @solana/kit. Pass { programAddress: account.owner } so each instruction goes to the program that owns its source. For a multisig authority, pass the co-signers with multiSigners.

As of @solana/spl-token 0.4.15 the legacy web3.js package has no WithdrawExcessLamports builder: the enum entry is commented out and misspelled WithdrawalExcessLamports upstream. Raydium hand-encodes a one-byte payload of 38. The package does ship createUnwrapLamportsInstruction.

SIMD-0392 (Activated; authors Igor Durovic and Jon C of Anza) lets an existing account stay below the current rent-exempt minimum if its pre-execution balance is above zero, its size does not grow and its owner does not change. The floor is then min(current minimum, pre-execution balance). Growth or an owner change requires the current minimum. Chainstack dates its mainnet activation at slot 443,664,000. This grandfathering makes a later rate increase non-disruptive.

Rent-exemption for token accounts, mints and multisigs dates from SPL issue 328 (opened 2020-08-26, closed 2020-08-27 via PR 342). The maintainers noted that 'with the new CloseAccount instruction, you can reclaim your SOL from a token account at any time', and gave wrapped SOL accounts a rent_exempt_reserve field in the Account struct. The current token program still stores that reserve in is_native.

Token and Token-2022 token accounts, mints and multisigs can return excess rent without being closed via the WithdrawExcessLamports instruction (discriminator 38). The account stays open, keeps its token balance and drops to the current minimum. Required signer: the token account owner, the mint authority, or the multisig signers; a mint with no mint authority needs the mint account itself to sign.

Excess rent has no deadline: it stays in the account, and reclaiming early does not block a later sweep. Each later step over-funds the account again, so the reclaimable excess grows from step to step.

Closing an SPL token account (CloseAccount) deletes it and returns its full rent deposit to a destination account chosen by the owner or close authority. For ordinary token accounts the token balance must be zero first (burn or transfer out). Wrapped SOL accounts are the exception: closing them with a balance recovers both the rent and the underlying SOL.

Rollback safeguards exist: SIMD-0437 depends on SIMD-0392 (relaxed post-execution min-balance check) so rent can be raised back to 6,960 if state grows too fast; SIMD-0438 can reset the rate, and SIMD-0389 does so automatically. Per Chainstack, accounts whose balance was reduced stay valid after a reset only if they do not grow, change owner, or fall below their starting balance.

Only the program that owns an account can debit it, so excess rent on a program-owned account (PDA) stays until that program ships a reclaim instruction. A safe instruction verifies the account's owner and the authority's signature, reads the floor from Rent::get() at call time, moves only the excess, and credits exactly what it debits. System Program wallets have no separate excess to reclaim.

Never hardcode rent. Read the minimum from getMinimumBalanceForRentExemption(data_len) in clients or Rent::get()?.minimum_balance(data_len) in programs. The Foundation says rent is likely to change again. The Rent sysvar fields changed with SIMD-0194, so do not multiply sysvar fields yourself.
